title: ADH and Renal Water Handling
text:
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) is synthesized by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary in response to rising plasma osmolality. ADH acts on principal cells of the renal collecting duct, where it triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, increasing water reabsorption from the tubular filtrate back into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium.

To characterize this response, investigators studied 12 healthy adult volunteers across three controlled hydration conditions. In the WATER LOAD condition, subjects drank 20 mL/kg of water over 30 minutes. In the EUHYDRATED condition, subjects maintained normal fluid intake. In the DEHYDRATED condition, subjects abstained from fluids for 18 hours. For each condition, the investigators measured plasma osmolality, plasma ADH concentration, urine flow rate, and urine osmolality after a 60-minute equilibration period. Conditions were tested on separate days in randomized order, and each subject served as their own control. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR), estimated by inulin clearance, showed no statistically significant difference in the reported comparison (p = 0.42). Estimates and confidence intervals for the GFR differences are not supplied; this p-value does not establish equivalence or constant filtration.

The results (Table 1) showed that plasma osmolality rose progressively from the water-load to the dehydrated condition. Plasma ADH tracked this rise closely. As ADH increased, urine flow rate fell sharply while urine osmolality climbed, exceeding plasma osmolality only in the euhydrated and dehydrated states. In the water-load condition, urine was markedly hypo-osmotic relative to plasma, consistent with low ADH and reduced collecting-duct water permeability. Comparing total osmolality does not establish tonicity, which depends on effective osmoles and a specified membrane.

The pattern is consistent with ADH-mediated water conservation, but hydration changed several variables and ADH was not independently manipulated. The repeated-measures design reduces confounding by stable participant differences; it does not isolate the ADH pathway or exclude filtration changes. These are synthetic teaching data, not a report of an actual hydration study or a protocol for readers to perform.

table.caption: Table 1. Plasma and urine measurements across three hydration conditions (mean values, n = 12).

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which condition shows urine that is hypo-osmotic relative to the subjects' plasma?
options: Euhydrated only
Water load only
Both euhydrated and dehydrated
Dehydrated only
questions.explanation: Water-load urine has osmolality 65 mOsm/kg, below plasma at 281. The other two urine values, 620 and 1,180, exceed their corresponding plasma values. This compares total osmolality. Dilute urine is consistent with reduced ADH-dependent collecting-duct water permeability; it does not mean that the entire nephron reabsorbs no water.

distractors.why: Confuses high urine osmolality with being hypo-osmotic; euhydrated urine (620) exceeds plasma (288), so it is hyperosmotic.
Dehydrated urine (1180) is the most concentrated and far exceeds plasma; it is the most hyperosmotic, not hypo-osmotic.
Both of these have urine osmolality above plasma, so neither is hypo-osmotic; only water load qualifies.

questions.stem: Why is measuring GFR useful when interpreting differences in urine flow, even though the reported p = 0.42 cannot establish unchanged filtration?
options: To confirm that ADH secretion was suppressed during dehydration
To assess whether changes in filtration could contribute to differences in urine output
To show that plasma osmolality was the dependent variable
To demonstrate that the collecting duct was the only nephron segment involved
questions.explanation: Urine flow depends on filtration as well as tubular handling. A GFR measurement helps assess whether filtration changes could contribute. A nonsignificant comparison does not rule out an important difference, and constant GFR would not by itself establish identical filtered solute loads if plasma concentrations change. The table also cannot prove that only the collecting duct changed.

distractors.why: ADH rose with dehydration in Table 1; GFR measurement addresses filtration, not whether ADH was suppressed.
Inulin clearance assesses filtration. It does not establish unchanged GFR from this p-value or identify the collecting duct as the only segment with altered handling.
Hydration condition was manipulated and plasma osmolality was measured. Inulin clearance estimates GFR; it does not determine the role of plasma osmolality as an experimental variable.

questions.stem: The progressive rise in plasma ADH from the water-load to the dehydrated condition is best explained by which mechanism?
options: Reduced aquaporin-2 insertion feeding back to the hypothalamus
Decreased plasma osmolality stimulating posterior pituitary release
Increased plasma osmolality stimulating hypothalamic osmoreceptors
Increased GFR raising filtered sodium delivery to the macula densa
questions.explanation: ADH release is governed primarily by hypothalamic osmoreceptors that sense rising plasma osmolality. As subjects moved from water load (281 mOsm/kg) to dehydration (297 mOsm/kg), increasing osmolality stimulated these osmoreceptors, driving greater posterior pituitary release of ADH (0.5 to 7.8 pg/mL). This is exactly the trend in Table 1, where ADH tracks osmolality. The hormone then increases collecting-duct water reabsorption, concentrating urine and helping restore normal osmolality. Higher, not lower, osmolality is the stimulus, and the pathway is osmoreceptor-driven rather than dependent on GFR or aquaporin feedback.

distractors.why: Reverses the direction: decreased osmolality suppresses ADH; the data show ADH rising as osmolality rises.
GFR was constant and the macula densa primarily regulates renin/tubuloglomerular feedback, not osmoreceptor-driven ADH release.
Aquaporin-2 insertion is a downstream effect of ADH, not the upstream signal that controls hypothalamic ADH secretion.

questions.stem: Which design feature most directly reduces confounding by stable differences between participants when comparing hydration conditions?
options: Urine osmolality was measured in mOsm/kg
Subjects were healthy adults
Each subject served as their own control across conditions
The dehydrated condition lasted 18 hours
questions.explanation: Having each participant complete every condition allows within-person comparisons, reducing confounding by characteristics that remain stable across those visits. Randomized order addresses systematic sequence effects separately. This design does not independently manipulate ADH, eliminate time-varying confounders or establish generalizability beyond the sampled adults.

distractors.why: Restricting enrollment to healthy adults narrows the study population; it does not remove differences among those adults or establish generalizability to other populations.
Units of measurement are a reporting detail and do not affect the strength of a causal inference.
The 18-hour duration defines the condition but is not itself a control feature that isolates ADH's effect.

questions.stem: For a simplified physiological interpretation, assume similar GFR across conditions. Falling urine flow together with increasing urine osmolality is most consistent with which change?
options: Increased glomerular filtration with constant reabsorption
Equal reabsorption of water and solute throughout the nephron
Greater water reabsorption relative to osmole removal from the tubular fluid
Net secretion of water into the tubular lumen
questions.explanation: Removing proportionally more water than osmoles from tubular fluid leaves a smaller, more concentrated urine volume. Increased collecting-duct water permeability under ADH provides a physiological explanation. This is an interpretation under the stated assumption, not proof from p = 0.42; ADH can also affect urea handling, and the table does not localize all changes to one nephron segment.

distractors.why: GFR was held constant in the study, so increased filtration cannot explain the change.
Equal water and solute reabsorption would keep urine isotonic and would not raise urine osmolality so steeply.
Net water secretion would dilute and increase urine volume, the opposite of the observed concentration and volume drop.

title: Allele Frequencies of a Metabolic Disorder
text:
Consider a fictional, fully penetrant, single-locus metabolic disorder with two alleles. Individuals with aa are affected and Aa carriers are unaffected. This simplified model excludes de novo variants and other causes of the phenotype. Because carriers cannot be distinguished from homozygous dominant (AA) individuals by phenotype alone, population geneticists often estimate the carrier burden indirectly from the frequency of affected newborns, assuming the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE).

A research team studied a recessive metabolic disorder caused by a single locus across four geographically distinct island populations (Regions A-D) that have historically practiced little interbreeding with one another. In each region, the team screened 2,000 newborns using a validated enzyme assay that reliably identifies affected (aa) infants at birth. Carriers were not directly genotyped. For each region, the investigators recorded the number of affected newborns and used the affected frequency to estimate the recessive allele frequency (q) and the expected carrier frequency (2pq), assuming HWE held within each region (Table 1).

The team noted that the four island populations differed substantially in historical founder size and in rates of consanguineous (related-partner) marriage. To look for changes in affected frequency over time, the investigators repeated the screen in Region C a decade later and obtained no statistically significant change in affected frequency. Effect estimates and confidence intervals for this follow-up were not reported, so equivalence was not established. As a methodological check, they also pooled all 8,000 newborns into a single combined sample and recomputed an overall affected frequency, then compared the carrier frequency predicted from the pooled data against the average of the four region-specific carrier estimates.

The investigators emphasized that their carrier estimates depend on several HWE assumptions, including random mating, no selection at the locus, negligible migration between regions, and a large population size. They cautioned that violations of these assumptions in any single island could bias the inferred carrier frequency for that region. Consanguinity is a specific reason to question the within-region random-mating assumption. The synthetic counts support calculations conditional on the model; they are not direct carrier genotypes.

table.caption: Table 1. Affected newborn counts and Hardy-Weinberg estimates by region (N = 2,000 newborns each).

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, approximately how many carriers (Aa) would be expected among the 2,000 newborns screened in Region D?
options: 1,280 carriers
320 carriers
960 carriers
720 carriers
questions.explanation: Under the regional HWE assumption, Region D has carrier frequency 2pq = 0.480. Multiplying by 2,000 gives 960 expected carriers. The 320 affected newborns are aa, while 720 is the expected AA count in that region. The value 1,280 comes from the AA expectation in Region B. Keep genotype, region and denominator aligned.

distractors.why: Reports the affected (aa) count, confusing carriers with homozygous recessives.
Gives the homozygous dominant (p² x N) count instead of the heterozygous (2pq x N) count.
Pulls the AA count from the wrong region (B), not carriers in Region D.

questions.stem: In Region B, the recessive allele frequency q is 0.20. What fraction of all copies of the recessive allele a in that population are carried by unaffected (heterozygous) individuals rather than by affected individuals?
questions.explanation: Heterozygotes carry one a allele each; affected aa individuals carry two each. Per individual, the genotype frequencies are 2pq = 0.320 (carriers) and q² = 0.040 (affected). Allele copies from carriers = 1 x 0.320 = 0.320; from affected = 2 x 0.040 = 0.080. Total a copies = 0.400, which equals 2q = 0.40, as expected. The fraction in carriers = 0.320 / 0.400 = 0.80. When q is small, most recessive alleles are hidden in heterozygous carriers, which is why rare recessive alleles persist in a population despite selection against affected homozygotes.

distractors.why: Simply restates q rather than computing the share of alleles held by heterozygotes.
Assumes alleles split evenly, ignoring that carriers vastly outnumber affected individuals.
Overestimates by mishandling the factor-of-2 weighting for aa individuals' two alleles.

questions.stem: Assuming HWE within each region, why can applying a single HWE calculation to the pooled newborn sample misestimate its carrier frequency?
options: Genotyping error in the enzyme assay
Population structure can produce a heterozygote deficit relative to HWE at the pooled allele frequency, called the Wahlund effect
Incomplete penetrance of the recessive allele
Sampling bias from unequal regional sample sizes
questions.explanation: Under the regional assumptions, the equal-size regions have mean q = (0.10 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.40)/4 = 0.25 and mean heterozygote frequency 0.350. A randomly mating population with q = 0.25 would instead have 2pq = 0.375. Pooling structured populations thus produces a heterozygote deficit, or homozygote excess, relative to that HWE expectation: the Wahlund effect. Taking sqrt(600/8,000) = 0.274 and then obtaining 2pq about 0.398 incorrectly assumes pooled HWE. These conditional estimates illustrate the problem; without carrier genotypes they are not a direct empirical test of it.

distractors.why: Assay reliability is a measurement issue; pooling subpopulations does not test it.
Penetrance affects phenotype expression, not the structure-driven pooling discrepancy.
All regional samples are equal (2,000), so unequal sizes cannot drive the effect.

questions.stem: The follow-up in Region C reported no statistically significant change in affected frequency. Which conclusion is justified by that statement alone?
options: Substantial migration occurred between Region C and the others
No change in affected frequency was detected; constant allele or genotype frequencies were not established
The locus is subject to strong directional selection
Mating within the region is nonrandom
questions.explanation: The reported test did not detect a change in affected frequency during the observation period. It does not prove equality, stable allele frequencies, random mating, absent migration or absent selection. A useful stability claim would also need the estimated difference and uncertainty, and direct genotype evidence would avoid relying solely on affected counts.

distractors.why: The follow-up alone does not determine mating patterns. Nonrandom mating can coexist with stable affected counts.
A nonsignificant change in affected frequency does not establish strong directional selection or exclude it.
This result neither demonstrates nor rules out migration. Its genetic effect would also depend on the migrants and their allele frequencies.

questions.stem: Region D shows a markedly higher affected frequency than Region A. Given that the islands differ in founder size and consanguinity, which explanation is most consistent with the data and the disorder's inheritance?
options: The enzyme assay is more sensitive in Region D than in Region A
Region D has a higher mutation rate that converts a alleles to A alleles
A smaller founder population and higher consanguinity in Region D elevated the recessive allele frequency and homozygote production
Region D carriers express the disorder due to dominance of allele a
questions.explanation: The disorder is autosomal recessive, so only aa individuals are affected and carriers are unaffected, which eliminates the dominance explanation. A smaller founder population produces stronger genetic drift and founder effects that can raise an allele's frequency, and consanguineous mating increases homozygosity, both boosting the production of affected aa offspring. Region D's higher q (0.40 vs. 0.10 in Region A) and affected frequency are consistent with these forces. Differential assay sensitivity would be a measurement artifact, but the assay is described as validated and applied uniformly. A higher mutation rate converting a to A would lower, not raise, the recessive allele frequency, contradicting the observed increase.

distractors.why: Contradicts recessive inheritance; carriers are unaffected by definition here.
The assay is validated and applied uniformly, so sensitivity should not differ by region.
Converting a to A would reduce q, opposite to Region D's elevated allele frequency.

title: Fuel Switching During a Fasting Treadmill Test
text:
Whole-body fuel utilization can be estimated noninvasively using indirect calorimetry, which measures the volume of oxygen consumed (VO2) and carbon dioxide produced (VCO2). The respiratory exchange ratio (RER = VCO2/VO2) reflects the relative contribution of carbohydrate and fat to oxidative metabolism. Complete oxidation of glucose yields an RER of 1.0, whereas oxidation of a typical fatty acid yields an RER near 0.70, because fatty acids are more reduced and require more O2 per CO2 generated.

Investigators recruited 12 healthy, recreationally active adults to study how fasting duration affects substrate use during submaximal exercise. Each participant completed three identical 30-minute treadmill bouts at 50% of their predetermined maximal oxygen uptake, performed in randomized order on separate days after 4, 12, or 24 hours of fasting. Diet and sleep were standardized the day before each trial, and trials were separated by at least 72 hours. During the final 5 minutes of each bout, expired gases were collected and steady-state VO2, VCO2, and RER were recorded. Plasma was sampled immediately afterward for glucose, free fatty acids (FFA), and the ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate. Results appear in Table 1.

As fasting duration increased, RER fell progressively, indicating a shift away from carbohydrate and toward fat oxidation. This was accompanied by rising plasma FFA and beta-hydroxybutyrate and a modest decline in plasma glucose. Total VO2 during exercise was similar across conditions, consistent with the matched workload. The investigators concluded that prolonged fasting promotes adipose lipolysis and hepatic fatty acid oxidation, sparing limited glycogen and glucose reserves. They noted that the design did not include a measure of muscle glycogen content and that participants served as their own controls across the three fasting states.

table.caption: Table 1. Steady-state respiratory and plasma measurements during 30 min of treadmill exercise at 50% VO2max after three fasting durations (means, n = 12).

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which fasting condition reflects the greatest relative contribution of fat to oxidative metabolism?
options: All three were equal, because VO2 was unchanged
4-hour fast, because plasma glucose was highest
24-hour fast, because RER was lowest
12-hour fast, because FFA and glucose were intermediate
questions.explanation: RER (VCO2/VO2) approaches 1.0 when carbohydrate is the dominant fuel and approaches 0.70 when fat dominates, because fatty acids are highly reduced and consume more O2 per CO2 produced. The lowest RER therefore marks the greatest relative fat oxidation. In Table 1, RER falls from 0.91 (4 h) to 0.85 (12 h) to 0.78 (24 h), so the 24-hour fast shows the largest fat contribution. This matches the concurrent rise in plasma FFA (substrate) and beta-hydroxybutyrate (a product of hepatic fatty acid oxidation). Glucose level and unchanged VO2 do not indicate fuel mix; VO2 reflects total oxidative rate, not which substrate is burned.

distractors.why: Confuses high glucose with high fat oxidation; high glucose actually accompanies more carbohydrate use and a higher RER.
Picks the intermediate condition; intermediate values are not the maximum fat contribution.
Misreads unchanged VO2 (total oxidative rate, fixed by matched workload) as meaning fuel mix was identical.

questions.stem: The rise in plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate with longer fasting is most directly explained by increased:
options: Gluconeogenesis from glycerol in the liver
Pyruvate oxidation feeding the citric acid cycle
Hepatic ketogenesis from acetyl-CoA derived from fatty acid oxidation
Glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is a ketone body. During fasting, adipose lipolysis releases free fatty acids that undergo hepatic beta-oxidation, generating large amounts of acetyl-CoA. When oxaloacetate is diverted toward gluconeogenesis and acetyl-CoA exceeds citric acid cycle capacity, the liver condenses acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate). The data fit this: as fasting lengthens, FFA rises and beta-hydroxybutyrate rises in parallel. Muscle glycogenolysis produces glucose-6-phosphate for glycolysis, not ketones. Glycerol gluconeogenesis makes glucose, not ketone bodies. Increased pyruvate oxidation would reflect carbohydrate use (higher RER), the opposite of the observed trend.

distractors.why: Muscle glycogenolysis yields glucose-6-phosphate for ATP, not ketone bodies, and muscle lacks the enzymes for net ketogenesis.
Glycerol gluconeogenesis produces glucose; it does not generate ketone bodies.
Pyruvate oxidation indicates carbohydrate metabolism (higher RER), inconsistent with the falling RER and rising ketones.

questions.stem: Why did the investigators have each participant complete all three fasting conditions rather than assigning each person to a single condition?
options: To eliminate the need for a non-exercising control group
To increase the total sample size to 36 independent observations
To allow muscle glycogen to be measured indirectly
To use a within-subject design that controls for individual differences in fitness and metabolism
questions.explanation: This is a repeated-measures (within-subject, crossover) design: each participant serves as their own control across the three fasting states. Because baseline VO2max, body composition, and metabolic traits vary widely between people, having the same individuals experience every condition removes that between-person variability as a confounder, isolating the effect of fasting duration. The randomized order and 72-hour washout further guard against order and carryover effects. The trials are not 36 independent observations; they are correlated within person (n still 12). The design does not replace a control group conceptually, and it does nothing to measure glycogen, an acknowledged limitation.

distractors.why: Repeated measures on 12 people are not 36 independent observations; the trials are correlated within subject.
A within-subject design controls between-person variation; it does not address the absence of a resting control group.
The design gives no measure of muscle glycogen; the passage explicitly lists that as a limitation.

questions.stem: VO2 remained near 2.05 L/min across all three conditions. This observation primarily supports which conclusion?
options: Total energy expenditure during exercise was held roughly constant by matching workload
Carbohydrate oxidation was identical in all three conditions
Fat oxidation did not change across the fasting conditions
Participants reached maximal oxygen uptake in every trial
questions.explanation: VO2 reflects the total rate of oxidative ATP production, which scales with energy expenditure and was fixed here by exercising everyone at the same relative intensity (50% VO2max). The stable VO2 across conditions confirms the workload, and thus total oxidative demand, was successfully matched, an intended control. It does not reveal fuel mix; RER does that, and RER changed markedly. Because trials were at 50% of maximum, participants were not at VO2max. Carbohydrate and fat oxidation each shifted (RER fell), so neither was constant even though total VO2 was. Distinguishing total oxidative rate (VO2) from substrate selection (RER) is the key concept.

distractors.why: Constant VO2 says nothing about fuel mix; the falling RER shows fat oxidation actually increased.
Exercise was at 50% VO2max, so participants were well below maximal oxygen uptake.
The changing RER shows carbohydrate oxidation fell with fasting; total VO2 being constant does not make substrate use identical.

questions.stem: Which hormonal change best accounts for the combined pattern of rising plasma FFA, rising ketones, and falling glucose as fasting lengthens?
options: Decreased insulin with increased glucagon and catecholamines promoting lipolysis and ketogenesis
Unchanged hormone levels with effects driven purely by exercise
Increased insulin alone driving glucose uptake into adipose tissue
Increased insulin-to-glucagon ratio promoting fuel storage
questions.explanation: Prolonged fasting lowers blood glucose, which suppresses insulin and raises glucagon; exercise additionally raises catecholamines. A low insulin-to-glucagon ratio activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, driving lipolysis and the observed rise in plasma FFA. The delivered fatty acids feed hepatic beta-oxidation and ketogenesis, explaining the rise in beta-hydroxybutyrate, while reduced insulin and depleting glycogen contribute to the modest fall in glucose. A high insulin-to-glucagon ratio (option A) and insulin-driven adipose glucose uptake (option C) describe the fed state and would lower, not raise, FFA. Hormone levels clearly change across fasting durations, so the unchanged-hormone option is incorrect.

distractors.why: A high insulin/glucagon ratio favors storage and lipogenesis; it would lower FFA and ketones, opposite to the data.
Insulin promotes glucose uptake and inhibits lipolysis, so it cannot explain rising FFA and ketones during fasting.
Falling glucose during fasting necessarily shifts insulin and glucagon; hormones are not unchanged.

title: Encoding Depth and Word Recall
text:
Researchers examined how the type of processing performed during encoding affects later memory, building on the levels-of-processing framework, which holds that deeper, more meaningful (semantic) encoding produces stronger memory traces than shallow (structural or phonological) encoding.

Eighty undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of four orienting-task conditions (20 per condition). During the study phase, participants viewed 60 common trait adjectives presented one at a time for 3 seconds each. For each word, they answered a yes/no question that determined how the word was processed. In the Structural condition, participants judged whether the word was printed in capital letters. In the Phonological condition, they judged whether the word rhymed with a cue word. In the Semantic condition, they judged whether the word fit meaningfully into a sentence frame. In the Self-Reference condition, they judged whether the word described themselves. Participants were not told their memory would be tested (incidental encoding).

After a 10-minute filler task of arithmetic problems, all participants completed a surprise free-recall test: they wrote down as many of the 60 studied words as they could in 5 minutes. The dependent variable was the number of words correctly recalled. The experimenter who scored recall was blind to condition assignment.

Mean recall increased across the four conditions in the predicted direction (Table 1). A one-way ANOVA using the rounded summary values gives approximately F(3, 76) = 102.8, p < 0.001, under the usual independent-error and equal-variance assumptions. Tukey pairwise comparisons under that same model indicated that the Semantic and Self-Reference conditions each produced significantly more recall than the Structural and Phonological conditions, and the Self-Reference condition exceeded the Semantic condition. The Structural and Phonological conditions did not differ significantly from each other.

The researchers concluded that the assigned encoding tasks affected recall under the experimental assumptions, with presentation duration held fixed. The design does not show that time never matters or that every difference between the tasks was measured. They interpreted the Self-Reference advantage as evidence that linking material to one's self-concept provides an especially elaborate, well-organized retrieval structure.

table.caption: Table 1. Mean number of words correctly recalled (out of 60) by orienting-task condition (n = 20 per condition).
rows: Does the word fit the sentence?

questions.stem: The study's design most directly tests which prediction of the levels-of-processing framework?
options: Information held in sensory memory decays within milliseconds unless attended to
Memory capacity in short-term storage is limited to roughly seven items
Retrieval is most successful when retrieval cues match the encoding context
Deeper, more semantic encoding produces stronger memory than shallow encoding
questions.explanation: The assigned orienting tasks contrast structural, phonological, semantic, and self-related encoding while holding presentation time fixed. This tests the levels-of-processing prediction that meaning-based encoding can improve later recall relative to shallow encoding. Sensory-memory decay, short-term capacity, and matching retrieval context are different proposed mechanisms that this design does not directly manipulate.

distractors.why: Confuses the depth-of-processing manipulation with sensory memory decay, a separate memory concept.
Names encoding specificity/cue-matching, which the design does not vary; cues were the same test for all.
Invokes Miller's 7±2 STM capacity, irrelevant to a 60-item long-term free-recall task.

questions.stem: Why did the experimenters hold the 3-second presentation time constant across all four conditions?
options: To create a longer delay before the free-recall test
To ensure participants reached the capacity limit of working memory
To increase the total number of words that could be presented in the study phase
To control presentation duration when comparing the assigned processing tasks
questions.explanation: Equal presentation time controls the exposure-duration explanation for a recall difference. Together with random assignment, this strengthens comparison of the assigned encoding tasks. It does not prove that every mental process or every participant is identical across conditions. The separate filler task sets the delay; list length is fixed; reaching a working-memory capacity limit is not the purpose.

distractors.why: Misreads constant timing as a way to fit more items, not as confound control.
Introduces working-memory capacity, which constant timing does not address.
Confuses presentation time with the 10-minute retention interval (filler task).

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, approximately what percentage of the 60 studied words did participants in the Self-Reference condition recall on average?
options: About 36%
About 27%
About 46%
About 15%
questions.explanation: Self-reference recall is 27.4 words out of 60, so 100 × 27.4/60 ≈ 45.7%, rounded to 46%. Reporting 27% confuses a word count with a percentage. The roughly 36% value belongs to semantic recall (21.8/60), and 15% belongs to structural recall (9.2/60).

distractors.why: Uses the Structural mean (9.2/60 = 15%) instead of the Self-Reference mean.
Reports the raw mean (27.4) as a percentage without dividing by 60.
Uses the Semantic mean (21.8/60 = 36%), an adjacent but incorrect row.

questions.stem: The approximate ANOVA F(3, 76) = 102.8, p < 0.001, together with the reported post-hoc comparisons, best supports which conclusion?
options: The Structural and Phonological conditions produced the strongest memory
At least one condition mean differed from the others, and deeper processing conditions outperformed shallow ones
Differences among the means were likely due to chance
Every condition differed significantly from every other condition
questions.explanation: The omnibus test provides evidence against all four population means being equal, under its assumptions; it does not identify every differing pair. The reported post-hoc comparisons support higher recall in semantic and self-reference conditions than in the two shallow conditions, while structural and phonological did not differ significantly. A small p-value describes how unusual this statistic would be under the equal-means null and model assumptions; it is not the probability that chance caused the result.

distractors.why: Overstates results; Structural vs. Phonological was explicitly nonsignificant.
Contradicts Table 1, where shallow conditions had the lowest recall means.
The small p-value indicates incompatibility with the equal-means null under the model assumptions. It is not the probability that chance caused the observed differences.

questions.stem: The superior recall in the Self-Reference condition is best explained by which memory principle?
options: Elaborative encoding that integrates items with an organized self-schema
State-dependent retrieval based on matching internal mood states
Proactive interference from previously learned material
Maintenance rehearsal that keeps items active in short-term memory
questions.explanation: Linking a word to an organized self-schema is an elaborative-encoding explanation for the self-reference advantage. The observation is consistent with that account without directly measuring the proposed retrieval structure. State-dependent retrieval concerns matching internal states, proactive interference concerns older learning disrupting newer material, and maintenance rehearsal is repetition; none is the assigned self-reference task described here.

distractors.why: Proactive interference hurts memory; it cannot explain superior recall.
Repetition can support retention, but simple maintenance rehearsal is not the meaning-based, self-related encoding manipulation described here.
State-dependent retrieval was not manipulated; mood states were not varied or matched.

title: Detecting Tones in Noise
text:
Signal detection theory distinguishes discrimination from a decision criterion under a specified model. In this synthetic auditory experiment, a faint 1000-Hz tone was either presented or absent against continuous white noise. Participants responded "tone present" or "tone absent."

Forty adults with normal hearing each completed 400 trials: four 100-trial blocks, each with 50 tone-present and 50 tone-absent trials in randomized order. Every participant experienced low (45 dB) and high (60 dB) background noise, crossed with liberal and conservative payoff conditions. Tone intensity was held at 50 dB using the same calibrated sound-pressure reference. Hits earned a bonus in both payoff conditions; false alarms were unpenalized in liberal blocks and penalized in conservative blocks. Block order was counterbalanced.

Table 1 contains illustrative pooled hit and false-alarm rates, not means of participant-level sensitivity estimates. Under an equal-variance Gaussian model, d-prime = z(hit rate) - z(false-alarm rate) and criterion c = -[z(hit rate) + z(false-alarm rate)]/2, where z is the inverse standard-normal cumulative function. Positive c is relatively conservative and negative c relatively liberal. The table derives both values from its displayed rates. Aggregating participants can conceal individual differences; inferential comparisons would use an appropriate participant-level model.

Higher noise is associated with the larger decrease in the displayed d-prime estimates. Liberal payoffs raise both hit and false-alarm rates and shift criterion toward "present." The d-prime estimates also vary somewhat with payoff, so these rounded results do not demonstrate exact sensitivity invariance. The model does not establish a unique receptor-level mechanism. Correct-trial reaction times are shorter in liberal blocks, but these means alone do not identify an evidence-accumulation threshold or measure a detection threshold across stimulus intensities.

table.caption: Table 1. Synthetic pooled response rates and derived equal-variance Gaussian indices, with mean correct-trial response time. Each block contains 2,000 signal and 2,000 no-signal trials across 40 participants.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which manipulation most strongly affected sensitivity (d-prime) rather than response bias?
options: Block order
Background noise level
Payoff structure
Reaction-time instructions
questions.explanation: At conservative payoffs, raising noise reduces d-prime from 2.05 to 1.17; at liberal payoffs, it falls from 1.93 to 1.04. Those differences are larger than the roughly 0.12–0.13 differences between payoff conditions at fixed noise. Noise therefore has the larger descriptive association with sensitivity here. Payoff primarily shifts criterion, but these data do not prove exactly unchanged sensitivity or identify a sensory pathway mechanism.

distractors.why: Payoff produces the larger change in criterion and a smaller change in the displayed d-prime estimates than noise. Exact sensitivity invariance is not established.
Counterbalancing addresses systematic order effects; the table is organized by noise and payoff and does not estimate a separate order effect.
No reaction-time instruction was manipulated; RT was only measured, so it cannot be the cause of sensitivity differences.

questions.stem: A reviewer worries that participants may have simply pressed 'present' more often in liberal blocks because they expected reward, not because they perceived the tone differently. Which feature of the design best addresses whether sensitivity truly differed across conditions?
options: Estimating d-prime and criterion from both hit and false-alarm rates under a stated signal-detection model
Counterbalancing block order across participants
Holding the tone intensity constant at 50 dB
Recruiting only participants with normal hearing
questions.explanation: Both hit and false-alarm rates are needed to distinguish discrimination from response tendency in the stated model. A lower criterion can raise both rates without requiring better sensitivity. Model assumptions and participant variation still matter; d-prime is not an assumption-free measurement of pure perception. A fixed tone, hearing screen or counterbalanced order alone does not make this distinction.

distractors.why: Counterbalancing controls practice and fatigue order effects; it does not separate perceptual sensitivity from response bias.
Normal-hearing screening improves sample homogeneity but does nothing to distinguish sensitivity from a willingness to say 'present'.
A constant tone level equates the physical signal but, on its own, cannot reveal whether response differences reflect bias versus sensitivity.

questions.stem: In the high-noise, liberal-payoff block, the hit rate is high but so is the false-alarm rate. This pattern is best described as the participant adopting:
options: A liberal criterion with relatively low sensitivity
A conservative criterion with high sensitivity
A liberal criterion with high sensitivity
An unbiased criterion with high sensitivity
questions.explanation: The high-noise liberal block has d-prime about 1.04 and c about -0.32. The negative criterion favors "present" responses relative to the equal-variance midpoint, while d-prime is lower than in the low-noise blocks. A high hit rate alone would not establish high sensitivity because false alarms also matter.

distractors.why: A conservative criterion lowers false alarms; the high false-alarm rate shows the opposite, and high noise lowers, not raises, sensitivity.
The calculated c is about -0.32, rather than zero, and sensitivity is relatively low. A false-alarm rate alone would not determine whether criterion is unbiased.
The criterion is correctly identified as liberal, but high noise reduces d-prime, so sensitivity is low, not high.

questions.stem: Raising the background noise from 45 dB to 60 dB lowered d-prime. This finding is most consistent with which concept from sensation and perception?
options: Sensory adaptation eliminating the receptor response entirely
Weber's law predicting a constant just-noticeable difference ratio
Auditory masking that reduces detectability of a fixed-intensity tone
Top-down processing overriding sensory input
questions.explanation: Increasing background noise makes the fixed-intensity tone harder to distinguish from tone-absent trials, consistent with auditory masking. The design does not vary tone intensity enough to estimate a threshold curve, and calling this an increase in an absolute threshold would overstate the measurement. Weber-type difference thresholds, complete sensory adaptation and a claim that top-down processing overrides all input are different accounts.

distractors.why: The noise manipulation changes stimulus conditions, but the table does not prove that top-down influences are absent. It directly supports reduced detectability, not complete top-down override.
Weber's law concerns the ratio for discriminating two suprathreshold stimuli, not detection of a signal buried in noise.
A lower d-prime does not show that receptor responses were eliminated; adaptation and masking are different concepts.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the clearest dependent variable in this study?
options: Background noise level
Payoff structure
The 2 x 2 within-subjects design
The sensitivity index d-prime
questions.explanation: A dependent variable is the measured outcome that the experimenters expect to change in response to their manipulations. Here the researchers manipulated noise level and payoff structure (the independent variables) and then measured outcomes such as hit rate, false-alarm rate, reaction time, and the sensitivity index d-prime. d-prime is computed from the data, not set by the experimenter, so it is a dependent variable. Noise level and payoff structure are the independent variables that were deliberately set across blocks. The 2 x 2 within-subjects description is the experimental design itself, not a variable that is measured. Therefore d-prime is the clearest dependent variable among the choices.

distractors.why: Background noise level was deliberately set by the experimenters, making it an independent variable, not a measured outcome.
Payoff structure was manipulated across blocks, so it is an independent variable rather than a dependent measure.
A 2 x 2 within-subjects design names the structure of the study; it is not a measured variable at all.

title: Conformity Under Vocal Dissent
text:
Researchers studied publicly stated judgments in a synthetic conformity experiment. Undergraduate participants (N = 240, 60 per condition) viewed pairs of dot patterns with a clearly discriminable difference in number. A designated incorrect answer was specified for each trial before testing. This relatively easy task permits a low private baseline error rate.

In Control, no confederates were present and participants answered privately. In Unanimous, six confederates all gave the designated incorrect answer aloud before the participant spoke. In Lone Ally, five gave that answer and one gave the accurate answer. In Anonymous, the same six unanimous confederates remained visibly present, but the participant used a private keypad whose response was not shown to the group. Participants were randomly assigned to conditions.

The primary measure was the mean proportion of trials matching the designated incorrect answer; in Control it is a baseline error rate rather than conformity to a group actually present. Before debriefing, participants who had matched the group on at least one trial were asked whether they privately believed the group's answer. The last column reports the percentage of those participants answering yes; its denominator differs from the trial-level response proportion.

Incorrect matching was highest with a unanimous public majority and lower with an accurate ally or private responses. Most questionnaire respondents did not report private agreement. This pattern supports a normative-influence account without proving motives or excluding informational influence. Private keypad responses also change response method relative to spoken answers; a further design would separate that change from answer privacy. Self-reports may reflect recall or social-desirability effects. All participants were debriefed after the questionnaire.

table.caption: Table 1. Conformity rate and private belief by experimental condition.
headers: Private belief among participants who matched at least once (%)

questions.stem: The pattern of results across conditions is most consistent with which type of social influence?
options: Obedience, because participants followed orders from an authority figure
Internalization, because participants permanently adopted the group's belief
Informational social influence, because participants used the group as a source of accurate information
Normative social influence, because conformity dropped sharply when responses were made privately
questions.explanation: Private responding reduces incorrect matching from 37% to 13%, and only a small fraction of questionnaire respondents report believing the group. That pattern is consistent with normative pressure producing public agreement without private acceptance. It does not prove a motive for every participant or rule out some informational influence. No authority issues commands, and lasting internalization was not measured.

distractors.why: Informational influence could contribute, but the privacy difference and limited reported private agreement more directly support normative pressure in this setup.
The task does not measure permanent belief change, and most respondents do not report private agreement. That does not support internalization as the main account.
Obedience requires an authority figure giving directives; the influence here comes from peer confederates, not authority.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers include the Control condition?
options: To serve as the independent variable in the experiment
To control for the effect of the post-task questionnaire
To increase the sample size and improve statistical power
To establish a baseline error rate against which conformity in social conditions can be compared
questions.explanation: Control estimates how often the designated incorrect answer is chosen without a group present. Its 4% rate provides a baseline for the relatively easy task. Comparisons with social conditions help assess the effect of each condition package, but subtracting the baseline does not identify every participant motive. Control is one level of the experimental manipulation, not a separate measure of the questionnaire effect.

distractors.why: A control condition's purpose is comparison, not adding power; power depends on per-group sample size and effect size.
Conditions are levels of the independent variable, not the IV itself; the control is one such level serving as baseline.
The questionnaire is the same across conditions and is not what the control isolates; the control isolates task difficulty.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, the introduction of a single accurate ally reduced the conformity rate by approximately what proportion relative to the Unanimous condition?
options: About 11%
About 26%
About 70%
About 50%
questions.explanation: Conformity was 37% in the Unanimous condition and 11% in the Lone Ally condition. The absolute drop is 37 - 11 = 26 percentage points. As a proportion of the Unanimous baseline, 26/37 is approximately 0.70, or about a 70% reduction. The question asks for the proportional reduction relative to the unanimous group, so the correct choice is about 70%. The 26% option confuses the absolute percentage-point drop with the proportional change. The 11% option simply restates the Lone Ally value. The 50% option underestimates the proportional decrease. This mirrors classic findings that breaking unanimity, even with one dissenter, dramatically undermines conformity pressure.

distractors.why: 11% is just the Lone Ally conformity rate, not a reduction; it ignores the comparison to 37%.
26 is the absolute percentage-point drop, not the proportional reduction the question requests.
50% understates the change; 26/37 is about 70%, not half.

questions.stem: The Anonymous condition keeps the confederates present but changes both response privacy and spoken versus keypad responding. Why can the study not isolate which of those changes reduced incorrect matching?
options: The reliability of the conformity measure
Random assignment of participants
The external validity of the dependent variable
A confound between two simultaneously changed factors
questions.explanation: Privacy and response method change together in the Anonymous comparison. Their individual contributions cannot be separated by that condition package, even with random assignment. The visible audience was not removed. A design independently varying privacy and response method would address the bundled-factor problem.

distractors.why: External validity concerns generalization; the issue here is internal, about which factor caused the effect.
Random assignment was performed and is unrelated; the problem is two factors bundled within one condition.
Reliability is measurement consistency; a confound can exist even with a perfectly reliable measure.

questions.stem: The post-task finding that most conforming participants did not privately believe the group's estimate best illustrates which distinction?
options: The difference between a stereotype and prejudice
The difference between an in-group and an out-group
The difference between the foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face techniques
The difference between compliance and internalization
questions.explanation: Publicly matching a group while reporting private disagreement illustrates compliance rather than internalization. The questionnaire is evidence about reported belief, not a perfect measure of lasting private attitudes. Stereotypes and prejudice, sequential-request techniques and social categorization refer to other distinctions.

distractors.why: Stereotype vs. prejudice is about belief vs. emotion toward groups, unrelated to public vs. private agreement.
These are sequential persuasion techniques; no escalating or shrinking requests were used in this study.
In-group/out-group is about social categorization, not the compliance-without-belief pattern shown.

title: Education, Neighborhoods, and Hypertension
text:
Researchers examined how socioeconomic status (SES) relates to cardiovascular health across a large U.S. metropolitan area. They recruited 4,800 adults aged 40-65 from neighborhoods that varied widely in median household income. Each participant completed a survey reporting educational attainment, household income, and self-rated chronic stress (a validated 0-30 scale, higher = more stress). Trained nurses, blind to participants' survey responses, measured resting blood pressure using a standardized protocol; the study-specific hypertension indicator was systolic pressure of at least 140 mmHg or current antihypertensive medication use. This simplified research indicator is not a complete current clinical diagnostic rule.

The team's central hypothesis drew on the fundamental cause theory of health disparities, which holds that higher-SES individuals can deploy flexible resources—knowledge, money, prestige, and beneficial social connections—to avoid disease risks regardless of the specific mechanisms operating in a given era. They predicted that hypertension prevalence would decline as educational attainment rose, and that this gradient would persist even after accounting for income.

Participants were grouped into four education strata. For each stratum, the researchers recorded hypertension prevalence, mean chronic-stress score, and the proportion living in a neighborhood lacking a full-service grocery store (a simplified grocery-availability proxy, not a complete measure of food access). Results appear in Table 1.

The investigators observed a clear inverse social gradient: each successive increase in education was associated with lower hypertension prevalence, lower mean stress, and a smaller share living without a neighborhood grocery store. Even within income brackets, more-educated participants showed lower hypertension prevalence, a pattern the authors interpreted as consistent with fundamental cause theory. Income adjustment alone does not isolate non-material resources or exclude other material resources, measurement error or residual confounding.

Because the data were cross-sectional, the authors cautioned that causal direction could not be firmly established and that unmeasured factors—such as early-life adversity or access to preventive care—might contribute to the observed associations. They called for longitudinal follow-up to clarify whether educational interventions could narrow cardiovascular disparities over time.

table.caption: Table 1. Hypertension prevalence, mean stress and neighborhood grocery availability by education (N = 4,800)

questions.stem: The researchers' prediction that the hypertension gradient would persist 'even after accounting for income' most directly reflects which theoretical claim?
options: That material deprivation is the sole driver of health disparities
That social mobility eliminates differences in health outcomes between strata
Multiple flexible resources associated with SES, including knowledge and connections, can shape health beyond measured income
That hypertension is primarily genetically determined within social classes
questions.explanation: Fundamental cause theory includes multiple flexible resources, such as knowledge, money, status and social connections. Predicting an education gradient after income adjustment is consistent with a role for resources beyond measured income. Such adjustment does not isolate those resources causally, make all remaining resources non-material or rule out residual confounding. The question asks which theoretical claim motivates the prediction.

distractors.why: The theory invokes several resources. Adjusting for measured income does not prove that material deprivation is absent, but it is not a claim that material deprivation is the sole pathway.
Genetics is never measured or invoked; fundamental cause theory emphasizes social resources, not heredity.
The persistence of the gradient shows differences remain, contradicting the claim that mobility erases them.

questions.stem: Having nurses who were blind to participants' survey responses measure blood pressure most directly served to reduce which threat to the study's validity?
options: Selection bias in recruiting participants
Observer (measurement) bias in the outcome
Confounding by household income
Attrition over the follow-up period
questions.explanation: Keeping nurses unaware of survey answers reduces the opportunity for expectations about education or stress to influence blood-pressure measurement. Blinding does not guarantee unbiased measurements, valid recruitment or adequate confounder adjustment. The design has a cross-sectional outcome assessment, so longitudinal loss to follow-up is not the issue targeted by this step.

distractors.why: Selection bias arises during recruitment, not during outcome measurement, so blinding nurses does not address it.
Assessor blinding does not remove confounding by income; adjustment may address measured differences under its assumptions but is not guaranteed to eliminate them.
Attrition requires longitudinal follow-up; this is a cross-sectional study with no repeated measurement.

questions.stem: Using Table 1, compare the absolute difference in hypertension prevalence between the lowest and highest education strata with the absolute difference in the share living without a neighborhood grocery store between those same strata. Which statement is correct?
options: The hypertension difference (~31.6 points) is slightly larger than the difference in grocery availability (~26.5 points)
The two differences are essentially equal (~26 points each)
The hypertension difference (~26.5 points) is slightly smaller than the difference in grocery availability (~31.6 points)
The hypertension difference is roughly twice the difference in grocery availability
questions.explanation: The hypertension prevalence gap is 48.6 - 22.1 = 26.5 percentage points. The grocery-availability proxy gap is 41.0 - 9.4 = 31.6 points. The first is smaller by 5.1 points. These are absolute differences between percentages, not relative risk reductions or causal effects.

distractors.why: Swaps the magnitudes: 31.6 is the gap in grocery availability and 26.5 the hypertension gap, and it reverses the direction.
The gaps differ by ~5 points (26.5 vs 31.6), so they are not essentially equal.
Twice 31.6 is ~63; the hypertension gap is 26.5, which is smaller than—not double—the gap in grocery availability.

questions.stem: The authors note that because the data were cross-sectional, causal direction 'could not be firmly established.' Which alternative interpretation does this caveat most directly leave open?
options: That the sample was too small to detect any association
That poorer cardiovascular health could limit educational attainment, rather than the reverse
That the blood-pressure measurements were unreliable
That hypertension and education are statistically independent
questions.explanation: Current measurements do not establish the full life-course ordering of education and health. Earlier health conditions or their determinants could have limited educational attainment, creating a reverse-direction or shared-cause explanation. This possibility requires a plausible timeline; it does not imply that current blood pressure changes past schooling. A large sample does not by itself guarantee power, reliable measurement or causal identification.

distractors.why: Reliability is a measurement issue addressed by the standardized protocol, unrelated to temporal ordering.
Sample size alone does not determine power, and the stated caveat concerns temporal ordering rather than a demonstrated lack of power.
The table shows a strong inverse gradient, so the variables are clearly associated, not independent.

questions.stem: The higher hypertension prevalence, higher stress and greater share without a neighborhood grocery store in successively lower education strata describe which concept?
options: The sick role
Spurious correlation
Cultural capital
A social gradient in health
questions.explanation: A stepwise association between social position and health outcomes is a social gradient in health. The table describes such a pattern across education strata. Naming it does not establish causality or rule out confounding. Cultural capital describes a resource, while the sick role describes social expectations around illness; neither names the graded pattern itself.

distractors.why: The sick role describes behavioral expectations of ill people, not a graded SES-health pattern.
Unmeasured confounding could contribute to the association, but spurious correlation is a proposed explanation rather than the descriptive name for the observed stepwise gradient.
Cultural capital is an SES resource, but it does not name the stepwise health pattern shown across strata.

title: Praise and Persistence in Children
text:
Researchers examined how different forms of adult feedback shape children's motivation and persistence after failure. The study drew on a distinction between praise directed at a stable trait ("You're so smart") and praise directed at effort or strategy ("You worked really hard"). Trait praise was hypothesized to foster a fixed mindset, in which ability is seen as unchangeable, whereas process praise was hypothesized to foster a growth mindset, in which ability is seen as malleable through effort.

A total of 160 children were tested individually: 80 in each age group, with 27 assigned to trait praise, 27 to process praise and 26 to neutral feedback within each age group. Each child first completed a set of easy puzzles and received one of three feedback types: trait praise, process praise, or neutral feedback ("You finished"). The neutral group served as a control. Children were then given a second, deliberately very difficult set of puzzles on which nearly all children failed. Finally, every child completed a third set matched in difficulty to the first set.

The study used a 3 (feedback) x 2 (age: 5-year-olds vs. 9-year-olds) between-subjects design, with children randomly assigned to feedback condition within each age group. After the difficult set, researchers recorded two outcomes: persistence, measured as minutes spent voluntarily attempting additional optional puzzles with no further praise or tangible reward offered, and performance change, measured as the difference in puzzles solved between the third set and the first set (a negative value indicates a drop).

Researchers also collected a self-report measure of task enjoyment on a 1-7 scale. To reduce experimenter bias, the adult delivering feedback was blind to the study's hypotheses, and all puzzles were pre-tested for difficulty. Outcomes are summarized in Table 1. The sample means are consistent with process praise supporting persistence and later performance in this setting. The trait-versus-process contrast is larger among 9-year-olds, but age was not randomly assigned and the table alone does not establish a developmental mechanism. Enjoyment comparisons were reported as nonsignificant, which does not establish equivalence. No mindset measure was collected, so the proposed mindset pathway remains an interpretation, not a demonstrated mediator.

table.caption: Table 1. Mean persistence, performance change, and enjoyment by feedback condition and age (SD in parentheses).

questions.stem: According to the passage, trait praise was hypothesized to foster a fixed mindset. Which belief best characterizes a child with a fixed mindset?
options: Failure provides useful information for adjusting strategy
Intelligence is a stable quality that cannot be substantially changed
Ability depends largely on the difficulty of the task
Effort is the main route to improving one's ability
questions.explanation: In the stated framework, a fixed mindset treats ability as relatively unchangeable. Trait praise was hypothesized to encourage that belief, but this experiment did not directly measure mindset, so the table does not establish that it mediated the feedback effects. Treating difficulty as informative or viewing strategy and effort as routes to improvement are different beliefs.

distractors.why: Describes a growth mindset (effort improves ability), the opposite of fixed.
Reflects growth-mindset framing of failure as informative feedback.
Externalizes ability to task difficulty rather than capturing a belief about self.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers include a neutral feedback group ('You finished')?
options: To serve as a control baseline against which praise effects could be compared
To increase the total sample size for statistical power
To manipulate the difficulty of the second puzzle set
To measure the children's baseline intelligence before the study
questions.explanation: Neutral feedback provides a comparison without the trait or process message. For 9-year-olds, mean persistence is 5.2 minutes under neutral feedback, between trait praise at 3.1 and process praise at 8.6. This helps distinguish differences relative to that baseline, rather than only comparing two praise types. Neutral feedback is still an intervention context, not necessarily the complete absence of social influence.

distractors.why: Confuses the logical role of a control with merely adding participants.
The difficulty manipulation was the hard second set, not the neutral group.
Neutral feedback was delivered after a task, not as a baseline IQ measure.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which comparison most directly supports the conclusion that process praise buffered children against failure-related performance declines among 9-year-olds?
options: Process praise (9 yr) enjoyment exceeded trait praise (9 yr) enjoyment
Process praise (9 yr) persistence exceeded process praise (5 yr) persistence
Neutral (9 yr) performance change was less negative than trait praise (5 yr)
Process praise (9 yr) showed +0.9 performance change versus -2.4 for trait praise (9 yr)
questions.explanation: Within 9-year-olds, the mean change is +0.9 puzzles for process praise and -2.4 for trait praise, a difference of 3.3 puzzles. This directly compares the relevant performance outcome and feedback conditions at the same age. Enjoyment and cross-age persistence comparisons answer different questions. The contrast supports a setting-specific interpretation without measuring the proposed mindset mechanism.

distractors.why: Uses enjoyment, which the passage says did not differ reliably.
Compares persistence across ages, an age effect, not buffering of performance.
Mixes age and condition, confounding the comparison.

questions.stem: The researchers intend optional puzzle time without further reward as a behavioral indicator of which concept, while recognizing that persistence can have other motives?
options: Extrinsic motivation driven by an external reward
Drive reduction following a physiological need
Intrinsic motivation reflected in voluntary task engagement
Incentive salience produced by a conditioned cue
questions.explanation: Voluntary task engagement without an additional reward can serve as an intended indicator of intrinsic interest. It is not a pure measurement of motive: prior praise, perceived expectations or a wish to succeed could also influence persistence. Operationalization specifies how a construct is represented, not proof that all alternative motives are absent.

distractors.why: The optional task offers no additional reward, so it is not designed as a direct external-payoff measure. Earlier feedback and perceived expectations could still influence engagement.
Drive reduction concerns physiological needs, not voluntary cognitive effort.
Incentive salience involves conditioned reward cues, not free engagement.

questions.stem: A critic argues that because the same adult delivered feedback to all children, the results might reflect that adult's behavior rather than the feedback type itself. Which study feature most directly addresses this concern?
options: Pre-testing all puzzles for difficulty before the study
Including two age groups in a between-subjects design
Random assignment of children to feedback condition within each age group
Keeping the feedback-delivering adult blind to the study's hypotheses
questions.explanation: Keeping the feedback provider unaware of the hypotheses reduces opportunities for deliberately or inadvertently steering children toward the predicted result. It does not guarantee identical tone or behavior across messages, since the provider knows what was said. Scripts and independent observation could strengthen the control. Randomization, task pretesting and age sampling address other design features.

distractors.why: Controls participant differences, not the experimenter's biased behavior.
Equalizes task difficulty but does not address experimenter conduct.
Addresses developmental generalizability, not experimenter bias.

title: Treating Insomnia: CBT-I vs. Pharmacotherapy
text:
Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) combines behavioral and cognitive methods, including stimulus control, individualized sleep scheduling and work on sleep-related beliefs. This fictional trial is a research-design exercise, not comparative clinical evidence or instructions for choosing or stopping treatment.

Adults with chronic insomnia (N = 240, 60 per group) were randomly assigned to CBT-I alone, a sedative-hypnotic medication alone, their combination or pill placebo. They kept daily sleep diaries. Mean sleep-onset latency (SOL), the reported time from lights-out to sleep, was measured at baseline, after eight weeks and at six-month follow-up. Supervised treatment ended after week eight; medication discontinuation followed a clinician-supervised plan, while participants could continue using learned behavioral skills.

Medication and placebo pills were visually matched and dispensed under concealed pill assignment. Participants and therapists knew whether behavioral therapy was provided. Diary assessors were unaware of group assignment. Matching pill appearance reduces some expectancy cues but cannot ensure successful blinding when effects or side effects reveal treatment. Similar baseline means do not prove equivalent groups or validate randomization by themselves.

The synthetic means in Table 1 show lower SOL after treatment in the active groups and the largest baseline-to-follow-up reduction for CBT-I alone. The medication-only mean rises between week eight and follow-up. Only these three time points were measured, so the table cannot show that one approach accelerated early relief. Variability, attrition and continued skill use are not quantified; the means do not establish statistical superiority, explain why individuals changed or isolate a specific learning mechanism.

table.caption: Table 1. Mean sleep-onset latency (minutes) by condition and time point.

questions.stem: Which feature of the study design most directly controls for participant expectancy (placebo) effects in evaluating the medication?
options: Keeping daily sleep diaries throughout the study
Use of visually identical placebo and medication pills
Random assignment of participants to the four conditions
Measuring sleep-onset latency at three time points
questions.explanation: Visually matched pills with concealed assignment reduce a cue that could create different treatment expectations between medication and placebo recipients. This does not guarantee that expectations were equal or blinding succeeded; experienced effects can reveal assignment. Randomization targets pre-existing group differences, while diaries and time points measure outcomes rather than directly matching expectations.

distractors.why: Confuses random assignment (controls baseline confounds/selection) with blinding (controls expectancy).
Sleep diaries are a measurement tool; they record outcomes but do not equalize participant beliefs.
Repeated measurement tracks change over time but does not address expectancy effects.

questions.stem: A reviewer notes that therapists delivering CBT-I could not be blinded to whether a participant received behavioral therapy. This unblinding is best described as a potential threat to:
options: The external validity of the sample
The reliability of the sleep-onset latency measure
Internal validity, via experimenter expectancy effects
The random assignment of participants
questions.explanation: Knowing which behavioral treatment is delivered can influence therapist behavior and participant expectations, threatening attribution to the intended treatment components. This is an internal-validity concern. It does not undo the random assignment itself. Blinded diary scoring addresses some observer effects but does not guarantee measurement reliability or eliminate bias in participants' own reports.

distractors.why: Random assignment happened before treatment and is not undone by therapist knowledge.
Blinded scoring does not establish test-retest or other reliability. The stated concern most directly involves differential treatment behavior and expectations.
External validity is about generalizing to other samples, not about therapist blinding.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which condition produced the greatest reduction in mean SOL from baseline to 6-month follow-up?
options: CBT-I + medication
Medication alone
CBT-I alone
Placebo
questions.explanation: The baseline-to-follow-up reductions are 33 minutes for CBT-I (62 - 29), 6 for medication (61 - 55), 25 for the combination (63 - 38) and 3 for placebo (60 - 57). CBT-I therefore has the largest reduction in the reported means. Without variability and follow-up information, this arithmetic does not establish population superiority or identify a mechanism.

distractors.why: Tempting because medication had a strong post-treatment value (24), but SOL rebounded to 55 at follow-up.
Combination improved durably (25 min) but less than CBT-I alone (33 min).
Placebo barely changed (60 to 57), the smallest reduction of all.

questions.stem: Which comparison most directly shows how much of the medication-alone group's post-treatment improvement was lost by follow-up?
options: CBT-I follow-up SOL (29) versus combination follow-up SOL (38)
Combination baseline SOL (63) versus CBT-I baseline SOL (62)
Medication-alone post-treatment SOL (24) versus its follow-up SOL (55)
Medication-alone post-treatment SOL (24) versus placebo post-treatment SOL (53)
questions.explanation: Medication-alone SOL rises from 24 minutes at week eight to 55 at follow-up, a 31-minute increase. This directly compares the end-of-treatment mean with the later mean. Relative to baseline 61, only a 6-minute mean reduction remains. These group averages do not establish that every participant relapsed or prove that stopping medication caused the change.

distractors.why: The medication-versus-placebo contrast at week eight concerns the initial end-of-treatment comparison rather than maintenance afterward.
This compares the CBT-I and combination groups at follow-up, not the medication-alone group across its follow-up interval.
Confirms comparable baselines but says nothing about durability of effects.

questions.stem: The investigators attribute CBT-I's durable effect to learning-based mechanisms. Which component of CBT-I best reflects principles of classical (respondent) conditioning?
options: Stimulus control that strengthens an association between the bed and sleep rather than wakeful arousal
Psychoeducation about normal sleep architecture
Setting goals and self-monitoring via daily sleep diaries
Cognitive restructuring of beliefs that one cannot function without sleep
questions.explanation: Stimulus control addresses learned associations between the sleep environment and wakeful arousal, making it the closest match to respondent-conditioning principles among these options. Cognitive restructuring focuses on beliefs, psychoeducation supplies information, and monitoring records behavior. This conceptual correspondence does not establish which component caused the synthetic trial pattern.

distractors.why: Targets maladaptive cognitions; cognitive, not associative classical conditioning.
Information transfer, not stimulus-stimulus association.
Self-monitoring and goal-setting reflect operant/self-regulatory, not classical, principles.
