title: Ionic Control of Neuronal Firing
text:
Resting membrane potential (Vm) and action potential firing depend on the unequal distribution of ions across the neuronal membrane and the selective permeability of ion channels. To probe how specific conductances shape excitability, researchers cultured rat hippocampal pyramidal neurons and recorded from individual cells using whole-cell patch clamp. Each neuron was held in standard artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF; control) containing 5 mM K+ and 145 mM Na+ in the bath, while the pipette (intracellular) solution contained 140 mM K+ and 10 mM Na+. Resting Vm and spontaneous firing rate were measured under control conditions and after the bath was switched to one of several test conditions.

In Condition 2, extracellular [K+] was raised to 20 mM. In Condition 3, the bath contained tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels. In Condition 4, the bath contained tetraethylammonium (TEA), which blocks many voltage-gated K+ channels. In Condition 5, the bath contained low-dose 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), another K+-channel blocker. After each manipulation, cells were allowed to stabilize for 3 min before a 30 s recording. Firing was evoked by holding cells at a fixed depolarizing current; spontaneous firing rate was quantified as spikes per second (Hz). Results are summarized in Table 1.

The investigators predicted, from the Nernst and Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz frameworks, that conditions raising the K+ equilibrium potential or reducing repolarizing K+ current would depolarize the cell and alter firing. They observed that elevating extracellular K+ depolarized Vm and increased firing, while blocking K+ efflux prolonged spikes and, at higher excitability, raised firing rate. TTX abolished action potentials entirely despite a near-normal resting Vm, confirming that voltage-gated Na+ channels are required for spike upstroke but contribute little to the resting potential. Figure 1 (not shown) plotted firing rate against measured Vm across conditions.

table.caption: Table 1. Resting membrane potential and firing rate of cultured hippocampal neurons under control and test conditions (mean values, n = 12 cells per condition).

questions.stem: In Condition 2, raising extracellular [K+] from 5 mM to 20 mM depolarized the resting Vm from -65 mV to -48 mV. This shift is best explained by which change?
options: The K+ equilibrium potential (E_K) became less negative, so K+ efflux at rest decreased
The Na+ equilibrium potential (E_Na) became more negative, increasing Na+ influx
Voltage-gated Na+ channels opened at rest, carrying sustained inward current
The Cl- equilibrium potential shifted, driving Cl- out of the cell
questions.explanation: By the Nernst equation, E_K = (61/z)log([K+]out/[K+]in). Raising [K+]out from 5 to 20 mM makes the ratio larger, so E_K becomes less negative (rises toward zero). At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+, so Vm sits near E_K; a less-negative E_K reduces the outward driving force on K+, decreasing K+ efflux and depolarizing the cell. The data match: Vm rose from -65 to -48 mV. Option B is wrong because E_Na is essentially unchanged. Option C contradicts the small magnitude and the resting context. Option D is unsupported and Cl- was not manipulated.

distractors.why: E_Na depends on extracellular Na+, which was unchanged; the depolarization is driven by K+, not Na+ equilibrium changes.
Voltage-gated Na+ channels are largely closed at rest and do not set the resting potential; a 17 mV shift is explained by K+ permeability, not tonic Na+ current.
Cl- was not altered, and Cl- typically has little net effect on resting Vm in these neurons; this is unsupported by the design.

questions.stem: In Condition 3, TTX reduced firing rate to 0 Hz while leaving resting Vm nearly unchanged (-63 mV vs -65 mV control). What does this dissociation most directly demonstrate?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels set the resting membrane potential
Voltage-gated Na+ channels are required for the action potential upstroke but contribute little to resting Vm
K+ channels are blocked by TTX, preventing repolarization
The Na+/K+ ATPase is inhibited by TTX, collapsing ion gradients
questions.explanation: TTX selectively blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, which mediate the rapid depolarizing upstroke of the action potential. With these channels blocked, no spikes can fire (0 Hz), yet resting Vm is nearly unchanged because the resting potential is set mainly by K+ leak conductance, not voltage-gated Na+ channels. This dissociation is the classic evidence that voltage-gated Na+ channels are essential for spike generation but negligible at rest. Option A is the opposite of the finding. Option C misidentifies TTX's target (it blocks Na+, not K+ channels). Option D is wrong: TTX does not inhibit the Na+/K+ pump, and gradients are preserved.

distractors.why: The near-normal resting Vm under TTX shows Na+ channels do NOT set the resting potential; this option states the reverse of the data.
TTX blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, not K+ channels; if K+ channels were blocked, repolarization would be impaired and resting Vm would likely depolarize.
TTX has no action on the Na+/K+ ATPase; the preserved resting Vm indicates gradients remain intact.

questions.stem: Conditions 4 and 5 each used a different K+-channel blocker (TEA and 4-AP) rather than a single blocker. What is the strongest methodological rationale for including both?
options: To increase the total sample size beyond what one drug allows
To test whether the firing effect generalizes across distinct K+-channel blockers rather than reflecting an off-target action of one drug
To create a positive control that guarantees firing rate increases
To control for changes in extracellular K+ concentration caused by the drugs
questions.explanation: Using two pharmacologically distinct K+-channel blockers (TEA and 4-AP) tests whether the observed effect on firing tracks the common mechanism, blockade of K+ efflux, rather than a drug-specific off-target action. Convergent results from independent blockers strengthen the causal inference that K+ conductance shapes firing. This is a replication-across-manipulations design principle. Option A is weak: each condition still has n = 12, and adding a drug is not how you boost a single group's n. Option C is wrong because a positive control is a separate concept and effects are not guaranteed. Option D is incorrect; the blockers act on channels, not by changing bath [K+].

distractors.why: Different drugs form separate conditions; they do not pool into one larger group, so sample-size augmentation is not the rationale.
A positive control is meant to confirm the assay can detect an effect; it does not 'guarantee' an increase, and that is not why two blockers were used.
TEA and 4-AP block channels rather than altering bath K+ concentration, so they do not serve as a control for extracellular [K+].

questions.stem: Using the firing-rate data in Table 1, which manipulation produced the largest increase in firing rate relative to control, and what is that increase?
options: High extracellular K+ (Condition 2); an increase of about 7 Hz
TTX (Condition 3); an increase of about 4 Hz
4-AP (Condition 5); an increase of about 3 Hz
TEA (Condition 4); an increase of about 9 Hz
questions.explanation: Control firing is 4 Hz. Condition 2 (high K+) reached 11 Hz, an increase of 11 - 4 = 7 Hz, the largest of any condition. Condition 4 (TEA) reached 9 Hz, an increase of 5 Hz (not 9). Condition 5 (4-AP) reached 7 Hz, an increase of 3 Hz. Condition 3 (TTX) fell to 0 Hz, a decrease of 4 Hz, not an increase. The high-K+ condition both depolarized Vm most (to -48 mV) and produced the greatest firing increase, consistent with depolarization bringing the cell closer to threshold. This question requires reading absolute values and computing differences from the control baseline.

distractors.why: TEA reached 9 Hz, but the increase over the 4 Hz control is 5 Hz, not 9 Hz; the option confuses the absolute rate with the change.
4-AP's increase (7 - 4 = 3 Hz) is correctly computed but is smaller than high-K+'s 7 Hz, so it is not the largest.
TTX reduced firing to 0 Hz, a decrease of 4 Hz, not an increase; it cannot be the largest increase.

questions.stem: TEA and 4-AP block voltage-gated K+ channels but did not abolish firing (9 Hz and 7 Hz). At the level of a single action potential, blocking these K+ channels would most directly be expected to:
options: Speed the depolarizing upstroke by increasing Na+ influx
Prolong the action potential by slowing repolarization
Hyperpolarize the resting membrane below -65 mV
Eliminate the refractory period by preventing Na+-channel inactivation
questions.explanation: Repolarization of the action potential is driven by delayed K+ efflux through voltage-gated K+ channels. Blocking these channels (TEA, 4-AP) slows K+ exit, so the membrane repolarizes more slowly and the spike is prolonged (broader). The data are consistent: both blockers depolarized resting Vm modestly (to -58 and -60 mV) and increased firing without abolishing spikes. Option A is wrong because K+ channels do not carry the upstroke; that is the voltage-gated Na+ current. Option C is wrong: blocking K+ efflux depolarizes, it does not hyperpolarize. Option D is incorrect because the refractory period depends largely on Na+-channel inactivation, which K+-channel block does not remove.

distractors.why: The upstroke is carried by voltage-gated Na+ channels; blocking K+ channels does not increase Na+ influx or speed the rising phase.
Reducing K+ efflux depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes; the table shows resting Vm rose to -58/-60 mV, consistent with depolarization.
The refractory period is set mainly by Na+-channel inactivation and recovery; blocking K+ channels does not eliminate it.

title: Hemodynamic Responses to Vasoactive Agents
text:
Clinicians distinguish two broad mechanisms for changing arterial blood pressure: altering cardiac output (CO), the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle per minute, and altering systemic vascular resistance (SVR), the total resistance the arterial tree imposes on flow. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is related to these quantities by MAP = (CO x SVR) + CVP, where CVP is the central venous pressure feeding the right heart. Because CO equals heart rate (HR) multiplied by stroke volume (SV), interventions can raise MAP either by increasing flow or by narrowing vessels.

To dissect these contributions, investigators anesthetized adult dogs (n = 12) and instrumented them with an aortic flow probe, an arterial catheter, and a central venous catheter. After a stabilization period, baseline HR, SV, MAP, and CVP were recorded. Each animal then received, on separate sessions in randomized order, after return to predefined baseline ranges for HR, SV, MAP and CVP, three infusions: norepinephrine (a mixed adrenergic agonist), sodium nitroprusside (a direct nitric-oxide donor), and a rapid 500-mL isotonic saline bolus. CO was computed from the flow probe and verified against HR x SV; SVR was calculated as (MAP - CVP)/CO and expressed in Wood units (WU). Group-mean values appear in Table 1.

The agents produced divergent profiles. Norepinephrine raised MAP despite a modest fall in CO, indicating that vasoconstriction, not increased flow, drove the pressure rise; a baroreflex-mediated decrease in HR accompanied this change. Nitroprusside lowered MAP and SVR while CO rose, consistent with reduced afterload. The saline bolus increased CO largely through enhanced SV (via the Frank-Starling mechanism) and elevated CVP, producing a smaller MAP increase than norepinephrine. MAP alone does not distinguish altered flow from altered resistance. Paired flow and pressure measurements describe that hemodynamic pattern, although they do not by themselves establish a molecular site of drug action. These are simplified synthetic profiles; the listed CO and SVR values are calculated from the displayed HR, SV and pressures, rather than independent group estimates.

table.caption: Table 1. Group-mean hemodynamic variables at baseline and during each intervention (n = 12).

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, the increase in MAP produced by norepinephrine is best attributed to:
options: An increase in cardiac output driven by a higher heart rate
An increase in systemic vascular resistance
A rise in central venous pressure
An increase in stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine raises MAP by 17 mmHg while CO falls from 5.04 to 4.62 L/min. Calculated SVR rises from about 17.5 to 22.5 WU, so greater resistance accounts for the pressure increase in this model. CVP contributes only a 1 mmHg change and SV is unchanged. The pattern is consistent with vasoconstriction and a compensatory baroreflex; the pressure equation alone does not prove receptor-level mechanisms.

distractors.why: CO fell rather than rose, and HR decreased, so increased flow cannot explain the higher MAP.
CVP rose only from 5 to 6 mmHg, a negligible contribution to the 17 mmHg MAP increase.
Measured SV remains 70 mL. The table therefore does not attribute the MAP increase to a larger stroke volume; it cannot exclude offsetting influences on filling and contractility.

questions.stem: The decrease in heart rate observed during norepinephrine infusion is most directly mediated by:
options: Direct beta-1 stimulation of the sinoatrial node
Decreased preload reducing sinoatrial firing
Withdrawal of sympathetic tone to the ventricles
Increased parasympathetic output via the baroreflex
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine raised MAP, which stretches carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors. The baroreflex responds to elevated pressure by increasing parasympathetic (vagal) output to the SA node and reducing sympathetic tone, slowing HR. This reflex bradycardia explains why HR fell from 72 to 66 despite norepinephrine's intrinsic beta-1 chronotropic activity; the baroreflex effect dominated. The reflex is the standard explanation for the bradycardia seen with potent vasoconstrictors. Direct SA-node stimulation would raise HR, the opposite of the observed change.

distractors.why: Beta-1 stimulation would increase HR, contradicting the observed decrease.
Sympathetic withdrawal to ventricles affects contractility, not primarily SA nodal rate, and is not the direct mediator of the bradycardia.
Preload (CVP) actually rose slightly; reduced preload was not the trigger, and the reflex acts through autonomic pathways.

questions.stem: Which design feature most directly addresses systematic order and carryover effects of the interventions?
options: Recording a baseline before any infusion
Randomizing session order and requiring return to predefined baseline ranges between interventions
Verifying CO against the product of HR and SV
Using a within-subject (repeated-measures) protocol
questions.explanation: Randomizing session order reduces systematic association between an intervention and its position in the sequence. Separate sessions with return to predefined baselines reduce carryover concerns. They do not guarantee no residual effect, so adequacy still needs assessment. Within-subject comparisons reduce stable between-animal differences but do not by themselves control order.

distractors.why: A baseline provides a comparison point but does not address the order in which subsequent agents are given.
Cross-validating CO addresses measurement accuracy, not sequence-related bias.
Repeated measures reduce confounding by stable animal differences. Order and carryover still need separate design controls.

questions.stem: Compared with norepinephrine, the saline bolus increased CO primarily by:
options: Increasing stroke volume through greater ventricular filling
Decreasing systemic vascular resistance
Increasing myocardial contractility independent of preload
Increasing heart rate through direct nodal stimulation
questions.explanation: After saline, HR rises from 72 to 78 (about 8%) and SV from 70 to 95 mL (about 36%). The larger proportional SV increase is the main arithmetic contributor to higher CO. Added volume and the supplied model support a Frank-Starling explanation, while reduced afterload may also contribute. CVP alone is not a direct measure of ventricular volume or proof of preload responsiveness.

distractors.why: HR rose only from 72 to 78; SV showed the far larger change, so rate was not the main driver.
Lower resistance can reduce afterload and contribute to SV. However, the requested HR-versus-SV decomposition identifies the larger SV change as the main contributor to increased CO.
Saline expands volume and raises preload; it does not provide a preload-independent inotropic stimulus.

questions.stem: Using the data for nitroprusside (CO = 6.40 L/min, MAP = 70 mmHg, CVP = 4 mmHg), the calculated SVR in Wood units is approximately:
options: 6.4 WU
questions.explanation: SVR in Wood units equals the pressure gradient across the systemic circulation divided by cardiac output: SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO. Substituting nitroprusside values gives (70 - 4)/6.40 = 66/6.40 = 10.3 WU, matching Table 1. This low resistance reflects nitroprusside's action as a nitric-oxide donor that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, dropping SVR from the baseline 17.5 WU. The reduced afterload also explains why CO rose even though MAP fell. Forgetting to subtract CVP, dividing by the wrong CO, or confusing the agents produces the distractor figures.

distractors.why: 6.4 is the CO value, not a resistance; it ignores the formula entirely.
About 14 results from omitting CVP and dividing MAP by the wrong CO (e.g., 70/5.04 ~ 13.9), not the correct (MAP-CVP)/CO.
22.5 WU is the norepinephrine SVR, not nitroprusside's; this confuses the two agents.

title: Mapping Three Loci in Zebrafish
text:
Researchers studying fin and pigment development in zebrafish characterized three autosomal recessive mutations that are inherited together more often than expected by chance: stubby gill (sg), pale fin (pf), and notched tail (nt). To determine the order of these loci on their shared chromosome and the distances between them, the team performed a three-point testcross.

They first crossed a true-breeding wild-type stock to a true-breeding triple-mutant stock to generate trihybrid F1 fish. Each F1 fish carried all three mutant alleles on one homolog and all three wild-type alleles on the other. F1 fish were then testcrossed to triple-mutant (sg nt pf / sg nt pf) partners. Because the testcross parent contributes only recessive alleles, the phenotype of each offspring directly reports the allele combination of the gamete it received from the F1 parent.

The team scored 1,000 offspring and sorted them into eight phenotypic classes, which collapse into four reciprocal pairs (Table 1). The two most frequent classes matched the parental (nonrecombinant) arrangements. Two intermediate-frequency pairs reflected single crossovers, and the rarest pair reflected double crossovers. By comparing the parental classes to the rarest class, the investigators identified which gene had been "switched" relative to the parental chromosomes, allowing them to assign the middle gene.

Recombination frequencies were calculated for each interval, and map distances were expressed in centimorgans (cM), using the short-interval approximation that 1% recombination corresponds to about 1 cM. Unobserved multiple crossovers can make recombination frequency underestimate longer map distances. The investigators also compared the observed number of double-crossover offspring to the number predicted if crossovers in the two intervals occurred independently. Ten double-crossover offspring were observed versus eleven expected. This gives a small positive estimated interference value. Such a small observed difference may reflect sampling variation and does not by itself establish biological interference. The synthetic counts are used to construct a local genetic map, assuming complete penetrance, equal viability and reliable scoring of all offspring classes.

table.caption: Table 1. Phenotypic classes among 1,000 testcross offspring (mutant alleles shown; '+' = wild type)

questions.stem: Based on the parental and double-crossover classes in Table 1, what is the correct gene order?
options: sg – nt – pf
nt – sg – pf
sg – pf – nt
The three loci are unlinked and have no shared gene order
questions.explanation: The middle gene is identified by comparing the parental classes to the rarest (double-crossover) class, because a double crossover swaps only the middle gene relative to the parental arrangement. The parental gametes are 'sg nt pf' and '+ + +'. The double-crossover gametes are 'sg + pf' and '+ nt +.' Comparing 'sg nt pf' to 'sg + pf,' only the nt locus changed (nt to +), so nt sits between sg and pf. Therefore the order is sg – nt – pf. Left-right orientation is arbitrary, so its reverse (pf – nt – sg) would be equivalent, but only sg – nt – pf is offered, and it is the uniquely correct choice among the options.

distractors.why: The marked excess of parental classes in this supplied linkage model is inconsistent with treating the loci as independently assorting.
Places pf in the middle; pf is also unchanged in the double-crossover class, so it cannot be the middle gene.
Places sg in the middle and reverses outer genes; sg does not switch in the double crossover, so it is not central.

questions.stem: What is the map distance between the nt and pf loci?
options: 5.0 cM
questions.explanation: The nt-pf interval has 53 + 47 = 100 single-crossover offspring plus 6 + 4 = 10 double-crossover offspring. Each double crosses this interval too, so 110/1,000 = 11%, giving an estimated local distance of 11.0 cM. The sg-nt interval is 10.0 cM; adding the two interval estimates gives 21.0 cM. The outer-locus observed recombination fraction is smaller because doubles restore the parental outer-locus arrangement.

distractors.why: 10.0 cM is the sg–nt interval distance (90 single + 10 double = 100/1,000), not the nt–pf distance.
21.0 cM is the total sg–pf map distance (sum of both intervals), not the single nt–pf interval.
About 5% counts only one of the roughly 50-offspring reciprocal single-crossover classes. Both classes and the double crossovers are needed.

questions.stem: Eleven double-crossover offspring are expected under interval independence and ten are observed. What are the estimated coefficient of coincidence and descriptive interference sign?
options: 0.91, giving a positive estimated interference value without establishing significance
1.00, indicating independent crossovers
0.91, indicating no interference
1.10, indicating negative interference
questions.explanation: Expected doubles are 0.10 × 0.11 × 1,000 = 11. The estimated coefficient of coincidence is 10/11 = 0.91 and estimated interference is 1 - 0.91 = 0.09, a positive value. These are descriptive estimates from this sample. Ten rather than eleven events does not, without uncertainty analysis, demonstrate that crossover interference exists in the population.

distractors.why: Inverts the ratio (expected/observed) and misreads the direction; fewer observed doubles cannot indicate negative interference.
The coefficient is correctly calculated, but the descriptive interference estimate is 1 - 0.91, which is positive. Its biological significance remains unresolved.
The point estimate is 10/11, not 1.00. That numerical difference alone still does not establish departure from independence beyond sampling variation.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers testcross the F1 trihybrids to triple-mutant fish rather than crossing F1 fish to each other?
options: Testcrosses produce larger clutches than intercrosses in zebrafish
A triple-mutant parent contributes only recessive alleles, so each offspring's phenotype directly reveals the F1 gamete genotype
The triple mutant supplies dominant alleles needed to score recombinants
Crossing F1 fish to each other would prevent any recombination from occurring
questions.explanation: A testcross to a homozygous recessive (sg nt pf / sg nt pf) partner is the standard mapping design because the recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles. Whatever allele the F1 gamete carries is therefore expressed in the offspring's phenotype, so each offspring is an unambiguous readout of a single F1 gamete. An F1 × F1 intercross would mask genotypes: a dominant phenotype could arise from multiple underlying genotypes, making it impossible to count recombinant gametes directly. Recombination still occurs in both designs, and clutch size is not the rationale. The triple mutant contributes recessive, not dominant, alleles.

distractors.why: Clutch size is not the experimental rationale; the testcross is chosen for genotype readability, not yield.
Recombination occurs during meiosis in the F1 regardless of which fish it is mated to; the cross type does not prevent crossing over.
The triple mutant contributes recessive alleles, not dominant ones; that recessive contribution is precisely what makes the phenotype readable.

questions.stem: Suppose a fourth locus, dl, assorts independently of sg, nt, and pf. In an analogous testcross, what recombination frequency would dl show relative to sg?
options: Approximately 21%
Approximately 11%
Approximately 50%
questions.explanation: Under independent assortment and the stated scoring assumptions, the two parental and two recombinant gamete combinations are equally likely, so the expected recombinant fraction is 50%. Very distant loci on one chromosome can also approach this limit because multiple crossovers obscure linkage. A finite sample can deviate around the expected fraction. The 21 cM summed local map is not the observed recombination fraction of the outer loci and does not apply to an independently assorting locus.

distractors.why: 0% indicates complete linkage with no recombination, the opposite of independent assortment.
21 cM is the sum of the two local map intervals, not the expected recombinant fraction for an independently assorting locus.
11% is the nt–pf interval distance; an independently assorting locus would recombine far more frequently (~50%).

title: Framing and Treatment Choice
text:
Decisions under uncertainty are sensitive to how options are described, even when the underlying outcomes are mathematically identical. Researchers investigated whether the framing of medical statistics shifts treatment preferences and whether prompting deliberation reduces this shift.

Adults (N = 320) read a vignette about a hypothetical surgery for a serious illness and then chose between "surgery" and "radiation." Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two description conditions. In the gain-frame condition, the surgical outcome was stated as a survival rate ("90 out of 100 patients are alive 30 days after surgery"). In the loss-frame condition, the same outcome was stated as a mortality rate ("10 out of 100 patients have died by 30 days after surgery"). The same 100-patient denominator and 30-day endpoint were used in both frames. Radiation information was held constant: 80 out of 100 alive at 30 days, delivered without an operation; surgery involved an inpatient recovery period. The vignette was hypothetical and did not define an objectively correct personal treatment choice. Crossed with frame, participants were assigned to a fast condition (respond within 10 seconds) or a deliberate condition (wait 30 seconds before responding). This produced a 2 (frame) x 2 (response mode) between-subjects design.

The dependent measure was the percentage of participants choosing surgery. The researchers reasoned that because the loss frame makes mortality salient, it should reduce surgery choice relative to the gain frame, consistent with a framing account; the design does not separately estimate loss aversion or establish it as the unique mechanism. They further predicted that deliberation would attenuate the framing effect by engaging controlled, rule-based processing rather than fast, intuitive processing.

Results appear in Table 1. Within the fast condition, the gain frame produced substantially more surgery choices than the loss frame. The framing gap was smaller in the deliberate condition. A confidence rating (1-7) collected after each choice showed that participants in the fast condition reported higher confidence than those in the deliberate condition, despite no instruction about accuracy. The smaller framing gap under the waiting instruction is consistent with a dual-process interpretation, but waiting is not a direct measurement of controlled reasoning. No processing mediator was measured. Percentages are rounded, and confidence ratings describe subjective certainty rather than accuracy.

table.caption: Table 1. Percentage choosing surgery and mean post-choice confidence (1-7) by frame and response mode.

questions.stem: The difference in surgery choices between the gain and loss frames, despite identical underlying outcomes, is best explained as an example of:
options: the availability heuristic
the representativeness heuristic
the framing effect
functional fixedness
questions.explanation: The gain and loss descriptions refer to complementary outcomes for the same denominator and the same 30-day endpoint. Different choices under those equivalent descriptions illustrate a framing effect. The data do not uniquely identify loss aversion, an automatic process or any particular decision theory as its cause.

distractors.why: Availability refers to judging frequency by ease of recall, not by equivalent reword of the same statistic.
Representativeness involves matching to a prototype or stereotype, not identical-outcome wording differences.
Functional fixedness is a problem-solving limitation about object function, unrelated to statistical framing.

questions.stem: In the fast condition, by how many percentage points did the gain frame exceed the loss frame in surgery choices?
options: 34 points
44 points
12 points
22 points
questions.explanation: From Table 1, the fast/gain condition had 78% choosing surgery and the fast/loss condition had 44%. The difference is 78 - 44 = 34 percentage points. This is the largest framing gap in the table, consistent with the hypothesis that fast, intuitive responding amplifies framing. The deliberate condition shows a smaller gap (70 - 58 = 12 points), so 12 corresponds to deliberation, not the fast condition. The value 44 is the raw surgery percentage in the fast/loss cell, not a difference, and 22 does not match any pair of cells in the fast condition.

distractors.why: 12 points is the gain-minus-loss gap in the deliberate condition, not the fast condition.
22 points does not correspond to any frame difference within the fast condition.
44 is the surgery percentage in the fast/loss cell, not a difference between frames.

questions.stem: Which feature of the study most directly allows the researchers to attribute differences in surgery choice to the frame manipulation rather than to pre-existing differences between participants?
options: Use of a 1-7 confidence rating scale
Collecting confidence after the choice was made
Random assignment of participants to conditions
Holding the radiation outcome constant across conditions
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes treatment allocation independent of pre-existing participant characteristics in expectation, reducing systematic confounding. Chance imbalance can remain, and causal interpretation still depends on conduct, follow-up and measurement. Keeping radiation information fixed controls a vignette feature; it does not by itself address participant differences.

distractors.why: Constant radiation outcomes controls the stimulus but not participant-level confounds across groups.
The rating scale is a measurement choice for a secondary variable, not a control for group differences.
Post-choice timing concerns the confidence measure, not internal validity of the choice comparison.

questions.stem: The finding that the framing gap shrinks in the deliberate condition is most consistent with which account of cognition?
options: The Yerkes-Dodson law relating arousal to performance
Dual-process theory, in which controlled processing can override automatic responses
The mere-exposure effect increasing preference with repetition
Long-term potentiation strengthening synaptic connections
questions.explanation: The gap is 34 percentage points in the fast condition and 12 in the waiting condition. A dual-process account can interpret that attenuation as greater opportunity for controlled reasoning. The waiting instruction does not prove that such reasoning occurred or fully corrected a response; the remaining gap and unmeasured processes limit the inference.

distractors.why: Yerkes-Dodson links arousal to task performance, not deliberation reducing a framing bias.
Long-term potentiation is a memory mechanism, unrelated to controlled correction of intuitive choices.
Mere exposure concerns preference from repetition, which was not manipulated in this design.

questions.stem: A reviewer notes that fast-condition participants reported higher confidence (5.6 and 5.4) than deliberate-condition participants (4.8 and 4.9) despite no accuracy instructions. Which conclusion is best supported by the data as reported?
options: Faster responding caused lower decision accuracy
Higher confidence accompanied responses that were more susceptible to framing
Confidence was negatively correlated with the size of the framing effect
Deliberation eliminated the framing effect entirely
questions.explanation: The fast cells have higher average confidence and a larger between-frame choice gap than the deliberate cells. That is a descriptive condition-level association, not an individual confidence–accuracy relationship. No objectively correct treatment choice is defined. An ecological correlation can be computed from group summaries in some settings, but it would not establish the corresponding individual-level correlation or a causal link.

distractors.why: The task has no objectively correct answer, so accuracy cannot be inferred from the data.
The reported condition pattern does not support the proposed negative association. Group summaries would not by themselves identify an individual-level confidence–framing relationship.
A 12-point gap persists in the deliberate condition, so framing was reduced, not eliminated.

title: Habit Reversal for Trichotillomania
text:
Trichotillomania involves recurrent hair pulling and related impairment. Pulling can occur with different awareness and reinforcement patterns; reduced unpleasant arousal is one possible maintaining consequence, not a universal explanation. This synthetic teaching trial examines a habit-reversal training (HRT) package that includes awareness and competing-response training.

Ninety-six adults meeting the study criteria were randomly assigned equally to HRT, supportive therapy matched for contact time, or waitlist. The active groups attended weekly sessions for eight weeks; waitlisted participants completed assessments without those therapy sessions. In HRT, a clinician helped participants notice relevant cues and practice a physically incompatible hand response. Practicing that response alone does not establish differential reinforcement, which would require specifying a reinforcing contingency.

The primary measure was the Massachusetts General Hospital Hairpulling Scale (MGH-HPS), a 0–28 symptom-severity self-report. Blinded raters also counted visible hair-loss patches. An exploratory sensor subset compared logged candidate pulling movements with separately self-reported episode counts; the reported correlation was r = 0.81. These are related measurements, not interchangeable with the full symptom scale. Sensors can miss or misclassify movements, and correlation is not numerical agreement or proof of unbiased measurement.

Table 1 gives synthetic group means, with a common within-group SD supplied for each outcome and time point. A one-way ANOVA of week-eight MGH-HPS values gives approximately F(2, 93) = 50.5 under independent-error and equal-variance assumptions. Tukey comparisons under that model separate HRT from each control, while the two control means are not significantly separated. A test of change scores would additionally need within-person covariance. The results favor the HRT package within the model, but do not isolate its competing-response component, establish the reinforcement mechanism or provide clinical treatment evidence.

table.caption: Table 1. Synthetic group means (n = 32 each); final row specifies a common within-group SD for each displayed measure.

questions.stem: If a pulling response becomes more likely because it reduces unpleasant arousal, which learning principle describes that specified contingency?
options: Positive punishment
Positive reinforcement
Classical extinction
Negative reinforcement
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement means that removal or reduction of an aversive condition strengthens the response that produced it. That matches the contingency stated in the question. It does not establish that every instance of hair pulling has this function. Positive reinforcement adds a reinforcing consequence; punishment reduces a response, and classical extinction concerns a different learned relation.

distractors.why: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to decrease behavior; here the behavior increases and an aversive state is removed.
Extinction is a classical-conditioning process of response weakening; the scenario describes operant maintenance, not extinction.
Positive reinforcement requires adding a pleasant stimulus; the passage describes removing an unpleasant one.

questions.stem: Replacing hair pulling with a competing response (fist clenching) rather than simply telling clients to stop pulling reflects which behavioral concept?
options: Stimulus generalization
Training a competing response that is physically incompatible with pulling
Spontaneous recovery
Latent learning
questions.explanation: Practicing a hand response that cannot occur simultaneously with pulling is competing-response training. It is not automatically differential reinforcement of an alternative behavior, because the passage does not specify a consequence that reinforces the alternative. Generalization, spontaneous recovery and latent learning describe different processes.

distractors.why: Stimulus generalization is responding similarly to comparable stimuli, unrelated to substituting an incompatible behavior.
Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response, not the deliberate replacement of a behavior.
Latent learning is unreinforced learning shown later; it does not describe a competing-response strategy.

questions.stem: Why did the investigators include a supportive-therapy control matched for therapist contact time in addition to a waitlist control?
options: To increase the total sample size for greater power
Compare the HRT package with similar therapist contact, while leaving its individual active components unresolved
To create a placebo that participants could not distinguish from HRT
To randomize participants more evenly across the three groups
questions.explanation: A contact-matched supportive condition helps assess whether the HRT package differs from a program with similar therapist time. A waitlist alone does not provide that comparison. Matching time does not guarantee equal expectations, and HRT includes multiple components. A component or dismantling comparison would be needed to isolate the competing response itself.

distractors.why: Adding a condition for power alone would not require matching on contact time; the purpose is controlling a confound.
Participants could distinguish supportive therapy from HRT, so it is not a true indistinguishable placebo.
Even randomization is achieved by the random assignment procedure, not by the choice of a contact-matched control.

questions.stem: Using Table 1, the reduction in mean MGH-HPS score for the HRT group from baseline to week 8 is approximately what percentage of its baseline score?
questions.explanation: The HRT group fell from 19.8 to 9.4, a reduction of 10.4 points. Dividing the change by the baseline gives 10.4 / 19.8 = 0.525, or about 53%. This is the proportional improvement relative to where the group started, the standard way to express percent change. The 26% option corresponds to dividing the change by roughly double the baseline or confusing the supportive-therapy change. The 13% value approximates the supportive-therapy group's reduction (2.5 / 20.1). The 75% value overstates the improvement and does not match any computation from the table, making 53% the only figure consistent with the data.

distractors.why: About 13% is the supportive-therapy group's percent reduction (2.5/20.1), not HRT's.
26% roughly halves the correct value, as if dividing by twice the baseline; it misreads the change.
75% overstates the reduction; the change of 10.4 is just over half of 19.8, not three-quarters.

questions.stem: The exploratory correlation r = 0.81 between sensor candidate-event logs and separately reported episode counts supplies what kind of evidence?
options: The self-report has high test-retest reliability
The self-report demonstrates a causal effect of HRT
The self-report is free of any response bias
Convergent evidence for related episode measures, with measurement limitations still unresolved
questions.explanation: An association between different measurements of related behavior is convergent evidence. It does not establish agreement in event counts, absence of bias or complete validity of the separate MGH-HPS symptom scale. It is not a repeated administration of the same measure and does not estimate a treatment effect. Sensor classification quality and the subset sample also matter.

distractors.why: Test-retest reliability compares the same measure across time, not two distinct measures of one construct.
Correlation between two measures cannot establish that HRT caused any change; that requires the experimental comparison.
A strong correlation does not guarantee absence of bias; consistent bias could persist across both measures.

title: In-Group Bias and Attribution
text:
Researchers examined how group membership shapes the causal explanations people generate for others' behavior. Drawing on social identity theory, they predicted that observers would explain a target's positive behavior differently depending on whether the target belonged to the observer's own group (in-group) or a rival group (out-group).

Undergraduate participants (N = 240) were first assigned to one of two "perceptual styles" based on a bogus dot-estimation task, a minimal-group manipulation designed to create arbitrary group identities with no prior history or real stakes. Participants then read 12 vignettes describing a target student performing either a desirable behavior (e.g., returning a lost wallet) or an undesirable behavior (e.g., cheating on an exam). The target was identified as sharing the participant's perceptual style (in-group) or belonging to the other style (out-group).

After each vignette, participants rated, on a 1-7 scale, the extent to which the behavior reflected the target's stable disposition (a dispositional attribution) versus external circumstances. Higher scores indicate stronger dispositional attribution. The researchers computed mean dispositional ratings for each condition (Table 1).

The pattern in Table 1 reflects the ultimate attribution error: observers attributed in-group members' desirable behaviors to disposition but their undesirable behaviors to situation, while reversing this pattern for out-group members. The descriptive group-by-behavior contrast is 2.4 - (-2.5) = 4.9 scale points. Participant-level paired ratings and their covariance would be needed for the inferential repeated-measures analysis; no F statistic is supplied.

For a proposed follow-up, participants would be randomly assigned either to an explicit disclosure that group assignment was arbitrary or to a neutral instruction, then rate a new counterbalanced vignette set. The investigators predicted that the attribution pattern might persist after disclosure; follow-up results are not supplied. The pattern is consistent with social identity accounts, but self-esteem was not measured or manipulated. It therefore does not establish the proposed motivational mechanism.

table.caption: Table 1. Mean dispositional attribution ratings (1-7 scale) by target group and behavior type. Higher = stronger dispositional attribution. SD in parentheses.

questions.stem: The pattern in Table 1, in which in-group members' positive acts are attributed to disposition while their negative acts are attributed to the situation, is best described as an example of:
options: The ultimate attribution error
The self-serving bias
The just-world hypothesis
The fundamental attribution error applied uniformly to all targets
questions.explanation: The ultimate attribution error describes the group-level pattern in which observers credit in-group members' positive behaviors to stable internal dispositions and excuse their negative behaviors as situational, while doing the reverse for out-group members. This is exactly the crossover pattern in Table 1 (the in-group advantage is +2.4 for desirable acts and -2.5 for undesirable acts). The fundamental attribution error is the general tendency to overweight disposition for any actor, not a group-differentiated pattern. The just-world hypothesis concerns the belief that people get what they deserve. The self-serving bias applies to attributions about one's own outcomes, not judgments about other people.

distractors.why: The fundamental attribution error is not differentiated by group membership; the data show opposite attribution patterns across groups, which it cannot explain.
The just-world hypothesis concerns the belief that outcomes are deserved, not group-biased causal attributions for behavior.
Self-serving bias applies to attributions about one's own successes and failures, not to judgments of other people's behavior.

questions.stem: The use of a bogus dot-estimation task to assign participants to arbitrary groups is an example of which research strategy, and what is its main purpose?
options: A confound that should have been controlled before data collection
A demand characteristic that invalidates the dependent measure
A minimal-group paradigm, used to show bias arises even without real intergroup history or stakes
A double-blind procedure that eliminates experimenter bias
questions.explanation: The minimal-group strategy examines whether group-related attribution differences appear with newly assigned, arbitrary labels rather than a history of conflict. It reduces dependence on prior group relationships. It does not prove that categorization alone is the only cause or eliminate demand effects, measurement limitations or alternative motives. It is distinct from concealing treatment assignment in a double-blind design.

distractors.why: The arbitrary grouping is the intended independent variable manipulation, not an uncontrolled confounding variable.
Demand characteristics remain possible in a minimal-group study. Their possibility does not automatically invalidate the measure or change the name of the design strategy.
Double-blind refers to concealing condition from participants and experimenters; it is unrelated to how groups are formed here.

questions.stem: Within the in-group target condition, what is the approximate difference in mean dispositional ratings between desirable and undesirable behaviors, and what does it indicate?
options: About 2.5 points, indicating out-group members are judged more harshly
About 5.8 points, indicating a ceiling effect on the rating scale
About 2.7 points, indicating in-group positive acts are seen as far more dispositional than in-group negative acts
About 0.2 points, indicating behavior type had little effect for in-group targets
questions.explanation: Within the in-group row, the desirable-minus-undesirable difference is 5.8 - 3.1 = 2.7 points. Higher values indicate stronger dispositional ratings, so the positive acts receive more dispositional attribution in these means. A mean below seven does not by itself rule out a ceiling effect in the underlying distribution, but the single mean 5.8 is not the requested difference.

distractors.why: 0.2 grossly understates the 5.8 versus 3.1 gap; behavior type had a large effect for in-group targets.
2.5 is the in-group-minus-out-group difference for undesirable behavior (the bottom row of Table 1), not the within-in-group desirable-versus-undesirable difference asked about.
5.8 is a single cell mean, not the difference. A ceiling effect would require information about the distribution; the mean alone neither establishes nor excludes it.

questions.stem: The authors interpret favorable in-group attributions as protecting collective self-esteem. This interpretation most directly draws on which theory?
options: Social identity theory
Cognitive dissonance theory
Realistic conflict theory
Drive-reduction theory
questions.explanation: Social identity theory links part of self-concept to group membership and can explain motivation to view an in-group favorably. It is the theory most directly invoked by the authors' interpretation. No self-esteem measure or manipulation is supplied, so the attribution pattern does not demonstrate that motive or exclude other explanations.

distractors.why: Drive-reduction theory addresses biological drives and homeostasis, not group identity or collective self-esteem.
Cognitive dissonance involves tension from conflicting self-relevant cognitions, not enhancement of group-based esteem through attribution.
Realistic conflict theory requires competition over scarce resources, which the stakes-free minimal-group design specifically excludes.

questions.stem: Suppose the proposed disclosure follow-up found a similar attribution pattern among participants who understood that assignment was arbitrary. Which limited conclusion would it support?
options: The observed pattern need not require belief that group assignment reflects a genuine perceptual trait
Informing participants increased the bias relative to the original condition
The biased attributions require participants to believe their group is legitimately meaningful
The original interaction was likely a statistical artifact of the bogus task
questions.explanation: Persistence among participants who understood the disclosure would show that believing the assignment reflects a genuine perceptual trait is not necessary for that observed pattern. It would not prove that categorization is the sole mechanism, that the effect increased, or that the original result was an artifact. Similarity would need an effect estimate and uncertainty; absence of a significant difference would not prove equivalence.

distractors.why: Directly contradicted: the bias persisted even when the group was framed as random, so perceived legitimacy is not required.
The hypothetical persistence would not show that the original result was an artifact. Neither statistical significance nor replication by itself eliminates every alternative explanation.
Persistence does not establish an increase. Comparing effect magnitudes requires their estimated difference and uncertainty.

title: Neighborhood Origins and College Completion
text:
Sociologists studying intergenerational mobility examined how the neighborhood a person grew up in shapes later educational attainment, independent of family income. Drawing on the social reproduction tradition, researchers hypothesized that concentrated neighborhood disadvantage transmits inequality through mechanisms such as under-resourced schools, limited access to information about college, and weak ties to college-educated adults.

The team analyzed a longitudinal survey that tracked 6,200 children born between 1995 and 2000. Each child's census tract of residence at age 10 was classified as low-, medium-, or high-poverty based on the share of households below the federal poverty line. Families were independently sorted into income terciles measured at the same age, allowing descriptive comparisons within measured income strata. Such stratification does not separate causal neighborhood effects from all family-level resources. The outcome was completion of a four-year bachelor's degree by age 25, verified through educational records rather than self-report. The 6,200 are the complete-case analysis sample; information on earlier loss to follow-up and record-linkage errors is not supplied.

To probe mechanisms, the team also measured each respondent's "college-information access," an index built from survey items about whether the respondent had spoken with a school counselor, knew an adult who had attended college, and had visited a campus before age 18. Higher scores indicated greater access.

Table 1 reports the percentage of respondents completing a bachelor's degree, broken down by neighborhood poverty and family income tercile. Within every income tercile, degree completion declined as neighborhood poverty rose. Notably, children from middle-income families in high-poverty neighborhoods completed degrees at lower rates than children from low-income families in low-poverty neighborhoods, a pattern the authors described as evidence that place matters above and beyond household resources.

In an illustrative adjustment analysis using the same complete-case sample and a linear-probability model, adding the college-information index reduced the magnitude of the neighborhood coefficient by about 40%. This attenuation is consistent with a candidate mediation account, but is not a demonstrated percentage of the effect causally mediated. Temporal ordering, measurement quality and confounding of the exposure, mediator and outcome would need assessment. The researchers cautioned that families are not randomly assigned to neighborhoods, so unmeasured characteristics of parents who select into low-poverty areas could partly explain the findings. They called for experimental housing-mobility designs to strengthen causal claims.

table.caption: Table 1. Percentage completing a bachelor's degree by age 25, by neighborhood poverty level and family income tercile (N = 6,200).

questions.stem: The researchers' framing that neighborhood disadvantage transmits inequality across generations through under-resourced schools and weak ties to college-educated adults is most consistent with which sociological concept?
options: Meritocracy
Cultural relativism
Social mobility
Social reproduction
questions.explanation: Social reproduction theory holds that social and economic inequalities are transmitted from one generation to the next through institutions such as schools and through unequal access to social and cultural capital. The passage explicitly invokes this tradition and describes mechanisms (under-resourced schools, weak ties to college-educated adults) that reproduce disadvantage. Meritocracy assumes rewards track individual effort and ability, contradicting the passage's emphasis on structural origins. Social mobility refers to movement between social positions, which is the outcome being constrained, not the transmission mechanism. Cultural relativism is the idea that practices should be judged within their own cultural context, which is unrelated to intergenerational inequality.

distractors.why: Meritocracy attributes outcomes to individual merit, the opposite of the structural transmission the passage emphasizes.
Social mobility names the constrained outcome, not the mechanism that transmits inequality across generations.
Cultural relativism concerns judging cultures on their own terms and is irrelevant to intergenerational inequality.

questions.stem: Which comparison is the specific cross-income reversal highlighted in the passage, where the middle-income group has a lower completion rate than the bottom-income group?
options: Bottom-income children in low-poverty vs. high-poverty neighborhoods (28% vs. 11%)
Top-income vs. bottom-income children in low-poverty neighborhoods (62% vs. 28%)
Middle-income children in high-poverty neighborhoods vs. bottom-income children in low-poverty neighborhoods (19% vs. 28%)
Top-income children in low-poverty vs. high-poverty neighborhoods (62% vs. 34%)
questions.explanation: The highlighted comparison is middle income in high-poverty neighborhoods at 19% versus bottom income in low-poverty neighborhoods at 28%. It is a descriptive reversal of income rank. Comparisons within an income stratum also describe neighborhood-associated differences; this cross-income contrast is not uniquely superior for identifying a causal neighborhood effect, and neither design removes all confounding.

distractors.why: This compares neighborhoods within the top-income stratum, rather than middle- versus bottom-income groups.
This is a useful within-bottom-income neighborhood comparison, but it is not the cross-income reversal requested.
This contrasts income within low-poverty neighborhoods and follows the usual income ordering; it is not the highlighted reversal.

questions.stem: The authors note that families are not randomly assigned to neighborhoods and that unmeasured parental characteristics may explain the results. This concern is best described as:
options: Poor test-retest reliability of the degree measure
Selection bias (confounding) limiting causal inference
Low external validity
A demand characteristic in the survey
questions.explanation: Residential sorting can reflect resources, housing availability, constraints and family characteristics that also relate to later education. Such shared causes can confound the neighborhood–completion association. Longitudinal timing and administrative outcomes do not remove that concern; record errors and complete-case selection can also matter. A housing experiment would need to distinguish assignment, actual moves and compliance rather than assuming residence itself is perfectly randomized.

distractors.why: External validity is about generalizability; the authors' concern is internal validity of the causal claim.
Administrative verification does not automatically establish reliability, but the stated concern is confounding from residential sorting rather than repeated outcome measurement.
The stated concern is a common-cause explanation for neighborhood and education, not participants responding to perceived study expectations.

questions.stem: The authors propose that neighborhood conditions influence later information access, which in turn influences completion. What role does that proposed pathway assign to information access, even though coefficient attenuation alone cannot prove it?
options: A confounding variable that should be controlled away
A moderator that changes the strength of the effect across groups
An unreliable measure with high random error
A candidate mediator whose causal role still requires additional evidence
questions.explanation: In the proposed causal model, information access is a mediator: an intermediate step between neighborhood conditions and completion. A 40% reduction in an adjusted coefficient does not establish that pathway or the fraction of an effect causally mediated. Confounding, measurement error and model choices could also produce attenuation. A moderator instead describes variation in an effect across levels of another variable.

distractors.why: The proposed pathway assigns an intermediate role. Alternative confounding structures remain possible, but cannot be settled solely by observing coefficient attenuation.
A moderator alters effect strength across subgroups (interaction); 'accounting for' the association describes mediation, not moderation.
Nothing in the passage suggests high random error; the index is treated as a substantive mechanism.

questions.stem: A respondent grew up in a high-poverty neighborhood and explains that no one in their family had attended college, so they were unaware of financial-aid options or application deadlines. This account best illustrates a lack of which resource?
options: Achieved status
Reference group identification
Absolute deprivation of food and shelter
Cultural capital and social capital
questions.explanation: Cultural capital includes the knowledge, skills, and familiarity with institutions (such as how college admissions and financial aid work) that facilitate navigating dominant systems. Social capital refers to resources embedded in one's networks, such as knowing college-educated adults who can share information. The respondent lacks both: no familiarity with the college process and no network ties providing that knowledge, mirroring the passage's information-access mechanism. Absolute deprivation refers to lacking basic necessities like food and shelter, which is not the issue described. Achieved status is a position earned through effort and is not a resource type. Reference group identification concerns the group one compares oneself to, not access to institutional knowledge or networks.

distractors.why: Absolute deprivation concerns basic survival needs; the respondent's barrier is informational, not material subsistence.
Achieved status is an earned social position, not a resource one accesses to navigate institutions.
Reference group identification is about comparison groups, not access to institutional knowledge or networks.

title: A Decay Signal and Its Background
text:
A teaching laboratory constructed a synthetic dataset to practice separating a changing sample signal from detector background. The modeled sample contains one radioactive isotope with a constant decay constant. Geometry, sample containment and detector efficiency are assumed fixed for the numerical model. The model predicts N(t) = N₀(1/2)^(t/t½), and the corrected sample count rate is proportional to the undecayed population. No particular physical isotope is identified by the dataset.

At each time point, the investigators recorded three quantities: the raw sample count rate, the blank rate with the sample absent, and the raw rate from a separate reference source modeled as constant over this observation window. The same detector configuration was used for all readings. Table 1 gives idealized mean rates in counts per minute. The table does not provide a measure of variability, so it cannot support a confidence interval or a claim about measurement precision.

The investigators subtracted the blank from the sample rate before comparing times. They did not subtract a different percentage of the sample at each time, because the blank was an additive detector background in this model. They also inspected the reference readings for evidence of drift. A stable reference is useful evidence about instrument response under the tested conditions; it does not independently prove that the sample remained sealed or that the sample contained only one isotope.

The exercise asks which calculations follow from the supplied assumptions and which claims require additional evidence. In a physical experiment, containment checks, instrument calibration and a justified isotope model would matter. The same numerical decrease could otherwise be confused with loss of sample or a change in detection conditions. The dataset is for analytical reasoning and does not prescribe handling of radioactive material.

table.caption: Synthetic teaching data; values are idealized means.

questions.stem: After blank correction, what fraction of the initial sample signal remains at 8 hours?
questions.explanation: The corrected rates are 1010 − 10 = 1000 initially and 260 − 10 = 250 at 8 hours. Their ratio is 250/1000 = 0.25.

distractors.why: This approximates the uncorrected ratio and does not perform the specified blank correction.
This is the fraction at 4 hours rather than 8 hours.
This is the fraction lost, not the fraction remaining.

questions.stem: Under the supplied single-isotope model, the half-life is:
options: 2 h
4 h
8 h
questions.explanation: Corrected signal halves from 1000 to 500 over the first 4 hours and halves again over each subsequent 4-hour interval.

distractors.why: Two hours is half of the observed halving interval.
Eight hours contains two halvings, not one.
Twelve hours contains three halvings, not one.

questions.stem: What does the stable reference most directly help assess?
options: Whether the sample contains exactly one isotope
Whether every sample nucleus has the same decay time
Whether detector response changed during the readings
Whether no sample could have leaked
questions.explanation: A reference whose modeled activity is constant helps monitor changes in detector response. It does not by itself establish sample composition or containment.

distractors.why: Reference stability does not analyze the isotope composition of the separate sample.
Individual decay times remain stochastic; the reference does not synchronize them.
A separate reference does not monitor sample leakage.

questions.stem: If the initial modeled sample population doubled with all other assumptions fixed, the expected corrected rate at 8 hours would:
options: Remain 250 counts/min
Become 125 counts/min
Become 1000 counts/min
Become 500 counts/min
questions.explanation: The same remaining fraction applies to twice the starting population, so the corrected 8-hour rate doubles from 250 to 500 counts/min.

distractors.why: This ignores the doubled initial population.
This halves rather than doubles the rate.
This is four times the original 8-hour rate, not twice it.

questions.stem: Which additional claim is least supported by the table alone?
options: The blank is constant in the supplied mean values
The corrected rate falls by a factor of eight over 12 h
The model fits these idealized means
The measurements have a narrow confidence interval
questions.explanation: The table supplies means without trial variability, standard errors or an interval method. A confidence interval cannot be inferred from those means alone.

distractors.why: The listed blank means are all 10 counts/min.
The corrected rates change from 1000 to 125, a factor of eight.
The listed corrected values match successive halvings.

questions.stem: In a separate balanced beta-minus decay equation, a nucleus has A = 100 and Z = 45 before decay. The daughter has:
questions.explanation: Beta-minus conversion changes one neutron into a proton, preserving mass number A while increasing atomic number Z by one. This question concerns count balance, not whether that particular decay is energetically allowed.

distractors.why: Beta-minus decay does not remove a nucleon.
Decreasing Z describes the wrong conversion direction.
These changes do not conserve the stated beta-minus equation.

title: Testing a Thin-Lens Relationship
text:
A synthetic optics experiment tests a converging lens using a small illuminated object and a movable screen. The lens, object and screen are aligned on one optical axis. Distances are measured from the lens plane in centimeters. The exercise uses the real-is-positive convention: f and dₒ are positive for the converging lens and real object; dᵢ is positive for a real image on the outgoing-light side. The thin-lens model is 1/f = 1/dₒ + 1/dᵢ, with magnification m = −dᵢ/dₒ.

For each listed object position, the screen is moved to the sharpest image. Table 1 contains idealized paired measurements. All rows use the same lens, illumination wavelength and alignment. The values are exact teaching values rather than measured uncertainty estimates. A graph of y = 1/dᵢ against x = 1/dₒ would therefore test a linear rearrangement of the lens equation. Both axes would have units of cm⁻¹.

The investigator then considers placing the object 5 cm from the lens. A missing sharp screen image would have more than one possible explanation in a real apparatus, including alignment problems. Under the stated ideal lens model and verified geometry, however, the sign of the calculated image distance predicts whether a real image can be caught on a screen.

In a separate illumination comparison, the investigator asks how photon energy changes between two vacuum wavelengths. For that calculation use E = hc/λ with h and c constant. It is distinct from fitting the focal length: no claim that a real lens is free from wavelength-dependent behavior is made. The aim is to separate a model’s algebra, its assumptions and the observations that would be needed to test those assumptions.

table.caption: Synthetic teaching data; values are idealized means.

questions.stem: What focal length is consistent with the first row?
options: 5 cm
10 cm
15 cm
45 cm
questions.explanation: 1/f = 1/30 + 1/15 = 3/30 = 1/10 cm⁻¹, so f = 10 cm. Object and image distances are not added directly.

distractors.why: This is half the focal length implied by the reciprocal-distance sum.
Image distance alone is not the focal length for this finite object distance.
Adding distances directly does not apply the lens equation.

questions.stem: For the first row, magnification is:
questions.explanation: m = −15/30 = −0.5. The image is inverted and half the object height in the stated convention.

distractors.why: The magnitude is correct but the sign omits inversion.
This reverses the distance ratio.
This reverses the ratio and omits inversion.

questions.stem: The graph of 1/dᵢ versus 1/dₒ is predicted to have:
options: Slope −1 and intercept 0.10 cm⁻¹
Slope +1 and intercept 10 cm
Slope 0.10 cm⁻¹ and intercept −1
Slope −10 cm and intercept 1
questions.explanation: Rearrange to y = 1/f − x. The slope is the dimensionless value −1 and the vertical intercept is 1/f = 0.10 cm⁻¹.

distractors.why: Both slope sign and intercept units are inconsistent with the rearranged equation.
This interchanges the slope and intercept and their units.
Slope is a ratio of equal reciprocal-length units and should be dimensionless.

questions.stem: At dₒ = 5 cm with the same ideal f = 10 cm lens, what does the model predict?
options: A real image at +10 cm
A real image at +5 cm
No light leaves the lens
A virtual image at −10 cm
questions.explanation: 1/dᵢ = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10 cm⁻¹, giving dᵢ = −10 cm. A virtual image is not captured directly as a sharp image on the outgoing screen.

distractors.why: The reciprocal difference is negative, not positive.
This ignores the focal-length term.
Virtual-image formation does not mean light stops propagating.

questions.stem: Which feature of the design most directly helps isolate object-distance effects?
options: Using different lenses for each row
Keeping lens and illumination conditions fixed
Reporting only the largest measured distance
Omitting the sign convention
questions.explanation: Holding the lens and illumination conditions fixed limits alternative changes while object distance varies. It does not eliminate every possible measurement error.

distractors.why: Changing lenses would change focal length and introduce another explanation for image-distance differences.
Selecting only one large result does not control a variable.
The sign convention is necessary for interpretable algebra.

questions.stem: In the separate photon comparison, a 400 nm photon has what energy relative to an 800 nm photon?
options: Half as much
The same amount
Twice as much
Four times as much
questions.explanation: With E = hc/λ and common h and c, halving wavelength doubles photon energy. This calculation does not determine a real lens’s dispersion.

distractors.why: This reverses the inverse-wavelength relationship.
Photon energy changes with frequency or wavelength.
The relationship is inverse-linear, not inverse-square.

title: Temperature, Blanks and an Enzyme Assay
text:
A synthetic enzyme assay measures formation of an absorbing product at three reaction temperatures. Substrate concentration, enzyme amount, total volume, optical path length and buffer pH are held fixed. At each temperature the investigators run an enzyme-containing sample and a matched no-enzyme blank. The blank contains the other reagents and measures a background increase that can occur without the added enzyme. Table 1 gives idealized mean absorbances at the beginning and after 60 seconds.

For this exercise, absorbance remains within a validated linear range and the absorbing product obeys A = εlc at every tested temperature. Use ε = 10,000 L/(mol·cm) and l = 1.0 cm. The investigator defines enzyme-associated signal change as the sample’s change in absorbance minus the matched blank’s change over the same interval. This subtraction distinguishes the reaction-associated increase from the additive background specified by the model.

The numerical means represent repeated readings from one enzyme preparation. Such repeats can characterize consistency within that preparation if their variability is retained, but they do not create independent enzyme preparations. To evaluate reproducibility across preparations, the investigator would need separately prepared samples and an appropriate design. The means shown here do not supply error bars or evidence of statistical significance.

The 30 °C condition has the largest corrected change among the three tested conditions. This observation does not locate an exact temperature optimum across all possible temperatures, identify the molecular cause of the smaller 40 °C response, or prove that heating produced irreversible denaturation. Additional temperatures and targeted measurements would be needed for those claims. The exercise focuses on background correction, rate units and the boundaries of an experimental conclusion.

table.caption: Synthetic teaching data; values are idealized means.

questions.stem: At 30 °C, what is the enzyme-associated absorbance change over 60 s?
questions.explanation: The sample change is 0.34 − 0.10 = 0.24, and the blank change is 0.12 − 0.10 = 0.02. Subtracting changes gives 0.22.

distractors.why: This is the final raw sample absorbance, not a corrected change.
This subtracts the sample starting value but omits blank drift.
This is the final blank absorbance rather than a change.

questions.stem: Using the corrected 30 °C change, the approximate mean product-formation rate is:
options: 0.37 μmol/(L·s)
3.7 μmol/(L·s)
22 μmol/(L·s)
370 μmol/(L·s)
questions.explanation: Δc = 0.22/(10,000 × 1.0) = 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L = 22 μmol/L. Divide by 60 s to obtain about 0.367 μmol/(L·s).

distractors.why: This introduces a factor-of-ten error in concentration conversion or time division.
This is the concentration increase over the whole interval, not the per-second rate.
This introduces a factor-of-1000 error in the mol-to-μmol conversion or time scaling.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the supplied means?
options: 30 °C is the exact optimum at every possible temperature
The 40 °C enzyme has irreversibly denatured
Temperature has no relation to the measured change
The corrected rate is highest at 30 °C among the tested conditions
questions.explanation: The three corrected changes are 0.10, 0.22 and 0.04, so 30 °C is highest among these observations. Finer temperature sampling and mechanistic evidence would be needed for stronger claims.

distractors.why: Three tested temperatures do not establish a global or exact optimum.
A lower signal alone does not identify irreversible denaturation.
The idealized means differ across temperatures.

questions.stem: Why include a no-enzyme blank at each temperature?
options: To measure all possible differences between independent enzyme batches
To estimate background change under the matched condition
To force the corrected signal to be identical across temperatures
To remove the need to record elapsed time
questions.explanation: A matched blank estimates non-enzyme-associated background change in the specified condition. It does not replace independent replication, erase true effects or supply a time denominator.

distractors.why: A blank is not an independent enzyme preparation.
Blank subtraction is not a procedure for making all results equal.
A rate still requires the measurement interval.

questions.stem: What would more directly test reproducibility across enzyme preparations?
options: Rereading the same cuvette many times
Reporting more digits for the same mean
Repeating the designed comparison with independent preparations
Deleting the blank readings
questions.explanation: Independent preparations sample an additional source of variability. Repeated reads from one preparation do not by themselves establish reproducibility across preparations.

distractors.why: Repeated reads address within-preparation consistency rather than independent preparation variability.
Extra decimal places do not create new observations.
Removing the blank loses a control and adds no replication.

questions.stem: If the positive blank drift were omitted, the inferred enzyme-associated rate at 30 °C would be:
options: Overestimated
Underestimated
Necessarily unchanged
Negative
questions.explanation: Without subtraction, a change of 0.24 would be attributed to the enzyme instead of 0.22. The positive background therefore biases the inferred rate upward in this model.

distractors.why: The omitted contribution is positive, so the direction is upward rather than downward.
The blank changes by 0.02 and therefore affects the corrected result.
Both corrected and uncorrected sample increases are positive.
